Myanmar ruling gives new relevance to genocide convention and is ‘full of messages’ for Israel

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (973 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theguardian

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Hailed as ‘a rare moment of justice’, judges’ decision sets out a roadmap for assessing the question of intent.
  • Industry observers note that the international court of justice (ICJ) verdict making Myanmar the first country in history to be found guilty of committing genocide does not just deliver justice for Rohingya victims.
  • In their nine votes to six majority ruling, the panel of judges in The Hague set out a detailed roadmap for how the convention should be applied to real-world situations in which a government is accused of committing genocide against a whole population group, especially when it comes to assessing the question of intent.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hailed as ‘a rare moment of justice’, judges’ decision sets out a roadmap for assessing the question of intent.

Industry observers note that the international court of justice (ICJ) verdict making Myanmar the first country in history to be found guilty of committing genocide does not just deliver justice for Rohingya victims. It also gives the 1948 genocide convention new relevance in governing the actions of nation states.

In their nine votes to six majority ruling, the panel of judges in The Hague set out a detailed roadmap for how the convention should be applied to real-world situations in which a government is accused of committing genocide against a whole population group, especially when it comes to assessing the question of intent.

The lengthy judgment will have been read particularly carefully by Israel, the only other country currently before the ICJ accused of genocide.

It is also relevant to Germany, which has been brought before the court by Nicaragua on the accusation it has facilitated and failed to prevent genocide in Gaza.

“I think it’s a judgment that brings the genocide convention alive,” noted Philippe Sands, a leading human rights lawyer who was part of the Gambian legal team. “It gives the convention practical, real meaning. And if the alternative view had been taken, the convention would essentially become a dead letter.”.

Amnesty International’s secretary general, Agnès Callamard, called the ruling “a rare moment of justice for survivors, victims and their families”. But it was also an assertion of humanitarian law in an increasingly lawless world.

In a recent development, “This is a good day for international law. We needed it,” noted Dr Iva Vukušić, an assistant professor in international History at Utrecht University and a war crimes expert. “It is really important, clarifying a lot of law, and that’s going to be very helpful going forward.”.

There will be a spillover from this ruling to its sister tribunal in The Hague, the international criminal court (ICC), providing a benchmark for when genocide charges could be made against individual perpetrators.

In a recent development, the Trump administration, instinctively hostile to international legal institutions, is also watching critically. The US ambassador to the UN told the ICJ before this judgment not to “lower the legal threshold for proving genocide” lest it be “weaponised” against US and allied soldiers.

The court did not directly lower the standard for demonstrating genocide, and the Gambia – which brought the case to The Hague – did not ask it to.

Sources indicate that the judges kept the existing benchmark for judging genocide intent as the “only reasonable inference” of Myanmar’s actions and referred extensively to prior case law. But it went a long way towards clarifying how that standard should be applied in assessing atrocity crimes committed by states.

Before this case, only Serbia had faced the charge of genocide at the ICJ, in cases brought by Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. In the Bosnian ruling in 2007, Belgrade was found to have failed to prevent the 1995 genocide in Srebrenica, but in both cases it was cleared of committing the genocide directly.

The new ICJ judgment finds the Myanmar military directly responsible for genocide against the Rohingya, a Muslim minority targeted in a ferocious counterinsurgency campaign that reached its peak in 2017.

Industry observers note that in assessing the Myanmar campaign, the ICJ looked not just at the death toll of about 10,000 in assessing the scale of the atrocities, but at the total Rohingya population targeted in northern Rakhine state, 815,000 people. Significantly, it cast its net wider than just the death toll, considering mental damage done to the survivors, particularly victims of sexual violence, and the impact on reproduction in the Rohingya community.

Most importantly, the ICJ judgment provided a guide to interpreting the standard set by Serbian cases, in which a finding of genocide could be made only if there were not other plausible motives for mass killing.

In this judgment, the court ruled that Myanmar could have had other motives, such as the desire to displace or punish the Rohingya population, but that those motives could exist alongside genocidal intent. The judges noted genocidal intent was the “only reasonable inference” from the “totality” of evidence.

In justifying that conclusion the judges pointed to several factors that international law experts say are relevant to the Gaza case, which is now hearing written pleadings and is expected to take at least another three years.

The common factors include the targeting of children, which the court described as striking at the “foundation” of the Rohingya as a group – the ICJ stated up to 2,109 Rohingya children under the age of five had been killed, while more than 5,000 Palestinian children under five years old have been killed in the Gaza war.

Another incriminating factor cited by the court was the “bulldozing and large-scale terrain clearance” after the destruction of villages, followed by “rapid construction” including security installations, which has been the hallmark of Israeli army occupation of over 60% of the Gaza Strip.

“It’s full of messages for Israel,” mentioned William Schabas, an international law professor and expert on genocide at Middlesex University. “There are obvious differences, of course, the evidence will be different, but if you exchanged the word Myanmar with Israel, you wouldn’t have to change much in the judgment.”.

The fact that there were six dissenting voices on the bench suggested that substantial parts of the majority’s reasoning were not beyond dispute, and lawyers involved in the case cautioned that it did not necessarily mean that the same bench would find Israel guilty of genocide in Gaza. But the same lawyers added that the opposite was almost certainly true. If this case had failed, the case brought by South Africa against Israel would have been all but over.

Levent Alpöge says he worked with Claude to discover a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis.

A mathematician working for Anthropic claims to have discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis using Claude. According to the BBC, Levent Alpöge used Claude to create a detailed proof of the problem over the course of six weeks. "This problem has been the sacred object in mathematics for me since my childhood," Alpöge said in his announcement.

According to recent reports, in very simple terms, Bernhard Riemann proposed way back in 1859 that prime numbers' locations along the number line have a meaningful order. Prime numbers are whole numbers that cannot be divided by anything other than themselves and the number one, if you want them to produce another whole number. As Scientific American notes, the Riemann Hypothesis is often considered the most important unsolved problem in math. The Clay Mathematics Institute recognizes it as one of its Millennium Prize Problems and had promised $1 million to the one who can find the first correct solution for it.

Sources indicate that alpöge has presented his findings in a programming language called Lean that can be used to write and confirm mathematical proofs. He stated the complete proof is over 250,000 pages long. In October, OpenAI also posted hundreds of solutions to previously unsolved math problems, as well as progress towards some of them, including the Riemann Hypothesis. It could take some time to confirm those solutions, just as it could take time to confirm Alpöge's Claude proof. James Maynard, a University of Oxford in England mathematician, told The Newly introduced York Times he was "98 or 99 percent certain" that Alpöge's discovery is accurate. If it is, then Anthropic's AI has solved a 167-year-old problem that even the world's brightest minds couldn't.

Iraq university’s removal of male professors teaching women sparks weeks of protests

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The removal of male professors teaching female students at a university in southern Iraq has sparked protests and been criticised by activists as a Taliban-like gender segregation policy.
  • As many as 400 women are estimated to have joined protests over the past two weeks calling for the return of their professors at Al-Qadisiyah University in a move that appears to have surprised its administrators.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Al-Qadisiyah University’s move a sign of the country’s slide into a Taliban-like gender segregation, say activists.

The removal of male professors teaching female students at a university in southern Iraq has sparked protests and been criticised by activists as a Taliban-like gender segregation policy.

As many as 400 women are estimated to have joined protests over the past two weeks calling for the return of their professors at Al-Qadisiyah University in a move that appears to have surprised its administrators.

The university said the move was necessary to “prevent the mixing” of men and women and had been requested by the families of female students. But students said their families had known since before they enrolled that there were men on the teaching staff and supported their daughters’ protest.

Students said university bosses had mocked their protests and refused to discuss their concerns about the sudden loss of their academic supervisors. On social media, commentators also accused the women of seeking to keep male professors to “establish immoral relationships with them”.

“My classmates and I went to demonstrate, and the university president, Rahi al-Yasiri, blocked our path with his bodyguards, who then began making fun of us. He ordered them to take photographs of our faces, in an attempt to intimidate us and punish us later,” said Huda, 22, one of the female students.

Huda said the students tried to explain how men and women still worked together in society in Iraq. “Aren’t there doctors who treat both men and women? Why then do you prevent male professors from teaching us, too?” In response, Huda said Al-Yasiri replied: “Even if you hit your heads against the wall, I will not bring back the professors.”.

The students stated a large number of them were tied to graduation projects and research supervised by the professors. They said they had grown accustomed to their professors’ teaching methods, who also knew their students’ strengths and weaknesses, which made replacing them at this stage more complicated.

Female students said they had been told by the university that if they were not happy with the change, they should drop out.

An Iraqi-British feminist researcher, Balsam Mustafa, from the University of Cardiff, said the female students were “treated as if they are minors without the right to object to decisions affecting their academic lives”.

Mustafa said the removal of the male professors was a part of a worrying trend in women’s rights in the country, with “growing discussion about women’s clothing and chastity reflected in the celebration of female students who wear the abaya”.

An Iraqi lawyer and human rights activist, Israa Salman, remarked the restrictions on women was a “societal catastrophe”.

“Attempts are being made to suppress women’s talents and turn Iraqi society – a society that has produced remarkable minds and expertise, with women playing pioneering roles in many fields – into something resembling Kabul under Taliban rule.

“This contradicts Iraq’s constitution and the international treaties and conventions the country has signed and ratified,” stated Salman.

Produced in collaboration with Jummar, an independent Iraqi media platform.

They were fined $811m for conning detained migrants, but the scams didn't stop

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2020 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mildred Juarez was stuck in detention for a month after her friends sent her bail money to Libre Immigration Services.
  • Every morning for a month, Mildred Juarez woke up at five to be the first person in the showers at the immigration centre in Texas where she was being detained.
  • But every day, she was told her bond had not been paid.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mildred Juarez was stuck in detention for a month after her friends sent her bail money to Libre Immigration Services.

Every morning for a month, Mildred Juarez woke up at five to be the first person in the showers at the immigration centre in Texas where she was being detained. Her friends had paid her bail, and she wanted to look presentable when she was finally released.

But every day, she was told her bond had not been paid.

Industry observers note that juarez was confused. Her friends had wired $2,600 (Â£1,970) to a bond tech giant, Libre Immigration Services (LIS), that had been recommended by her lawyer. LIS remarked it would begin "the process of paying her immigration bond". But the next day came, and the day after that, with no release.

What she didn't know was that LIS was owned by a convicted fraudster, who had acquired the assets of another bail manufacturer co-founded by two men who also had fraud convictions. These two men were fined $811m in 2024 for scamming their clients.

Their firm, Libre By Nexus, which was at one point the largest immigration bail manufacturer in America, had appeared to shut down after federal regulators caught up with them.

But public records and BBC interviews with clients and former employees reveal a tangle of interconnected operations continued - along with the flow of cash - while leaving immigrants stuck in detention centres.

Sources indicate that since President Donald Trump has returned to office after promising an immigration crackdown, Immigrations and Customs Enforcement (ICE) has made over 1.2m arrests, and fast-tracked deportations. The administration has tried unsuccessfully to make it illegal to give migrants bail but the sharp increase in detentions has increased demand for bond companies to secure bail and their release.

Recent findings suggest that conditions in these centres can be poor. Held in custody, away from family, often scared to speak out, many have faced health problems and endured inadequate food or treatment, according to immigrant advocates and reports by the US government.

"He did everything right" - The impact of Trump's immigration crackdown in Ohio.

In the detention centre where Juarez was locked up, she and about 100 other detainees slept in bunks laid out in rows in a cacophonous room. The lights were left on all night and guards routinely woke everyone up for roll call. According to Castro and advocacy groups, detainees who caused trouble were put in "the hold" - solitary confinement.

The White House and officials from Homeland Security did not respond to the BBC's request for comment.

For Juarez, the wait to be bailed out of detention seemed interminable.

It has been revealed that in an email to the BBC, a spokesperson for LIS said Juarez "misunderstands" their services - that they are not bondsmen themselves, but they connect detained individuals to those who are licensed bondsmen. They said another company ultimately decided not to work with her.

According to recent reports, an email sent by LIS, and reviewed by the BBC, stated that the manufacturer had paid a cash bond to ICE on behalf of Juarez. The message was forwarded to Juarez as proof of payment a few days before her release.

But it was another bail agent, who was not affiliated with LIS, that got her out of detention - after her friends raised even more money to hire another tech giant.

"I was losing it inside there," Juarez recalled, using an expletive.

In a recent development, "I lost everything. When I was released I had nightmares I was back inside.".

Libre Immigration Services never paid back her deposit, despite sending messages promising a refund. A spokesperson told the BBC that they would refund Juarez's bail amount once her friend verified their details.

It is notoriously difficult for migrants like Juarez to make bail, which can be upwards of $7,000.

According to recent reports, once charged with illegal entry, a judge may grant bail, which allows the migrant to live freely while their case is heard, a process which can take years. Once a person's court case is completed, the bond amount is returned.

It has been revealed that bail agents, who are licensed to provide a down payment on bail and vouch that if the accused does not show up for court they will pay the rest, can help people get out of detention sooner. But many won't help migrants because they view them as too much of a flight risk. A 2024 government report found that a third of migrants not already in custody did not show up for court.

Libre by Nexus, also known as Nexus, was willing to take that risk.

Founded in 2013, its co-founders Michael Donovan and Richard Moore had served prison time in the 1990s and early 2000s for a string of fraud and forgery convictions.

Through his attorney, Donovan declined to comment. Moore did not respond to the BBC's request for comment.

Although people with felony convictions are barred from holding a bond licence in many states, Nexus operated as a kind of middleman between immigrant clients and licensed bondsmen.

Holed up in detention in Louisiana after crossing the border, Rosa Murillo heard about Libre by Nexus from another inmate, and the 18-year-old Honduran's mother called them to arrange her $7,000 bail.

A Nexus employee picked her up and took her to a hotel room where she was told she would have to pay $420 a month and wear a GPS ankle monitor until her case was completed.

Rosa Murillo states she was ashamed to wear the ankle bracelet that Nexus required.

Federal regulators accused Nexus of implying, in their contracts, that the GPS bracelets were court-mandated, when they were actually the private organization's requirement.

Murillo got a job as a waitress and tried to hide the ankle bracelet for fear that people might think she was a violent criminal.

Over the course of a decade, Libre by Nexus enabled more than 20,000 migrants like Murillo to be released on bail - and took in more than $230m in revenue, court documents show.

But the ankle bracelets were a constant source of annoyance for Nexus clients released from detention, according to two former employees who spoke to the BBC.

A former Nexus co-owner, Evan Ajin, told the BBC that the manufacturer stopped requiring released detainees to wear ankle bracelets in 2018.

When Mark Supetran worked for Libre by Nexus, he says he would tell people about how they had to wear an ankle bracelet.

But Mark Supetran, who was based in the Philippines and worked for the company for a few months in 2022, claims the bracelets were still in use when he worked for the company.

Sources indicate that supetran stated he would field 80 calls a day from people who were either going through the process themselves or were the loved one of someone who was. Telling them they would have to wear a tag on release was part of the conversation.

"Part of the script was to say something like: 'The client will be wearing an ankle monitor.' So that got me thinking, like, why?" he recalled. "It doesn't make sense, we're not the government.".

It has been revealed that not getting refunds of bail deposits was another complaint. Another former employee told the BBC he was instructed to tell callers that they would get their money back once their case was completed.

"But that that was never the case," he told the BBC. "I mean, you had people calling me in almost every day like 'Hey, am I gonna get my money back? Am I gonna get my money back?'".

Ajin, the former Nexus co-owner, told the BBC that the contract clearly stated that monthly fees did not go towards their bond, but were programme fees, and so they could issue no refund.

The US Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB), an agency created to stop predatory lending and other abusive financial practices, successfully sued Libre by Nexus and its parent company.

The lawsuit accused the firm of running a "predatory immigrant-services scam" that trapped victims into paying high, long-term fees. Nexus also misrepresented and concealed the terms, the lawsuit alleged, such as the non-refundable, monthly payments.

The judgment sided with the CFPB and a federal judge found the firm liable for using predatory tactics against its clients in 2024, fining Nexus, its parent company, Ajin, Donovan and Moore $811m.

In addition to the hefty fine, the judge forbade the tech giant from collecting on past debts.

Days after the 2024 order, Donovan sold a number of the company's assets, including customer lists and records - for $3.50.

As part of the agreement the buyer would also take on its debt.

Ajin says he ceased contact with everyone involved following the sale.

In a recent development, moore is now in prison, after being convicted of filing fraudulent Nexus taxes. He and Donovan, who is also behind bars, are awaiting sentencing for insurance fraud and conspiracy. Donovan has also been charged with sexually abusing a boy under 12, but has not entered a plea in that case.

The purchaser of Nexus's assets was a Pennsylvania businessman named Vincent Smith, who had been sentenced to 10 months' probation in 2015 for conspiring with employees to write over $2m in fake bail bonds.

Smith called the upcoming business Libre Immigration Services.

This March, the judge who issued the fine also ruled the sale of the company had violated her order by transferring the debts.

Judge Elizabeth Dillon voided the sale, but did not shut Libre Immigration Services down. She is due to review claims that LIS also violated the order by trying to build an app to collect debts from Nexus's old clients.

A former paralegal at Nexus, who went on to work for LIS, told the BBC about the app. She mentioned after the sale, the lines between the two companies were blurred.

Another employee confirmed her account independently to the BBC, noting that the app was never finished because they could not obtain the client data.

A hearing date has not been set, and LIS has denied any wrongdoing, noting the firm was never in possession of the client lists.

A screenshot of Libre Immigration Service's website.

Libre Immigration Services continues to solicit immigrant clients and advertises its services online and on social media.

Its website features glossy photos of beaming families alongside the promise to "get your loved one released from a detention centre today!".

In a recent development, that wasn't Janie Aviles's experience. She had wired Libre Immigration Services $10,000 to help get her friend out of detention in Texas. But LIS did not pay his bail, Aviles said, until a month later, leaving him, like Juarez, in limbo.

When she called they offered various explanations and then stopped answering the telephone, she said.

It has been revealed that eventually she drove to the office listed on the website, which had shown a picture of LIS's logo hanging above the door. But on arrival, she found there was no storefront with the business's name and logo anywhere.

According to recent reports, she stated the company finally paid the bail a month after getting the funds, after she had reported them to the district attorney. No charges have been laid.

An LIS spokesperson mentioned that "verification of significant information had to occur to prevent or minimise loss".

According to recent reports, "The application was ultimately approved, and the cash bond was pledged to ICE. Presumably any delay related to the substantial bond amount and the heightened requirements of review.".

They also stated the office at that location was for business operations, and not client services, and that a sign had been ordered and would be installed, pending permits.

But the ordeal was enough to anger Aviles, who feared for her friend while he was stuck in detention. "I'm like 'This ain't right.'".

Anker combines style and substance with this versatile power bank that packs a whopping 25,000-mAh capacity and is capable of delivering up to 165 watts to two devices (100 watts for a single device connected via USB-C). I love the rounded edges, the retractable, flat 2.3-foot USB-C cable up top, and the clever braided 1-foot USB-C cable that doubles as a carry loop. It has a display to show the remaining battery, charging rate in and out, battery temperature, and health. It supports pass-through charging and takes around two hours to recharge.

OK, you don’t really need this many stats, but having a precise idea of how much power remains is useful and reassuring. I love the built-in cables, because they ensure you’re never caught without one. This is also below the limit for power banks on flights, so you can travel with it. Anker’s Laptop Power Bank fast-charged everything I tested it with, including multiple smartphones, an iPad, a Poco tablet, a MacBook Air, and a Chromebook. You can charge four devices simultaneously without any concerns. After a year of use, mine still performs perfectly.

Industry observers note that you don’t always need massive capacity, and you don’t always have room for a big power bank. If you want something more portable, go for the Nimble Champ Pro. At 6.2 ounces, it’s one of the lightest on the market. It’s smaller than a deck of cards and can deliver 20 watts to charge two devices at once via a USB-C port on either end. It feels durable, comes in a snazzy upcoming range of speckled color finishes, and has a bright lanyard loop that makes for easy carrying and helps you pick it out of your backpack. The Pro version is bigger but doubles the capacity (to 20,000 mAh) and has a similar design with two USB-C ports that go up to 65 watts. There’s also a smaller version with a 5,200-mAh capacity that tops out at 15 watts.

Industry observers note that another reason I like Nimble is its environmental efforts. Batteries are not environmentally benign. They use lithium, cobalt, and other rare metals whose supply chains are environmentally and socially questionable at best. But Nimble’s use of bioplastics and plastic-free minimal packaging at least reduces the environmental impact where it can be reduced. This version uses 90 percent recycled plastic (up 25 percent from the original) and comes in smaller plastic-free packaging. Nimble includes a 3.3-foot USB-C to USB-C cable in the box.

The original was the first Qi2 power bank I tested and was my top pick for quite a while, but this sequel is even better. The Qi2 wireless charging standard borrows elements of Apple’s MagSafe, enabling supported phones to connect with perfect alignment using a ring of magnets. Because it works with Apple's StandBy mode, you can stick Qi2 or MagSafe phones in portrait or landscape orientation.

Sources indicate that qi2 brings faster wireless charging rates of up to 25 watts, but it is also backward compatible, so older Qi devices can still charge (albeit more slowly). This compact portable charger has a handy kickstand, a two-way USB-C port on the left edge, and a power button with an LED display that can show remaining power as a percentage. It can also display charging time when plugged in, watts out, temperature, and battery health. Anker offers the device in a range of fun colors (I love the burgundy). Anker has added vents on top and bottom with a cooling fan you can turn off for silent mode. It is slimmer and lighter than the original and can charge faster, but it's also more expensive.

In a recent development, despite a large capacity, it falls short of two full charges for your iPhone when charging wirelessly. You might squeeze out a little more if you plug in the short USB-C cable provided. It’s also quite bulky, but if you have an iPhone or another Qi2 phone, we recommend several slimmer alternatives in our Best Qi2 and MagSafe Power Banks guide.

Recent findings suggest that maybe you want a large-capacity power bank that can handle all your portable gadgets, but you’re tired of gray bricks. I am a sucker for Sharge’s transparent designs and cyberpunk aesthetic, but this prism-shaped power bank is more than just a pretty face. With a maximum output of 170 watts, a whopping 24,000-mAh capacity, and an IP66 rating for water resistance (fine in the rain, but best not to submerge), the Sharge 170 has form and function. The smart display highlights battery life as a percentage, time remaining, and the input or output in watts. It supports many standards, including Power Delivery 3.1, Quick Charge 4.0, and PPS, and it fast-charged most of the devices I tested, including the iPhone 15 Pro, Pixel 8, Xiaomi 14 Ultra, and MacBook Air. You can simultaneously charge three devices at fast speeds.

According to recent reports, the box includes a braided USB-C cable and a somewhat pointless wee velvety bag (does anyone use these?). It can recharge completely in an hour via USB-C at up to 140 watts (with the right cable and charger). I’ve tested some of Sharge’s newer power banks, but I still prefer the 170. The triangular design is unique and means the display is always angled perfectly to glance at. You are paying a premium for the aesthetic, but I’ve used mine often over the last few months. It’s built to last.

Recent findings suggest that my Apple Watch usually makes it to bedtime, but for super busy days and overnight trips, it’s nice to have a power bank capable of charging it up. This Anker power bank has a handy pop-up Apple Watch charger that can deliver 5 watts and supports Nightstand mode. It also has a built-in USB-C cable and a USB-C port, so you can deliver up to 30 watts to your phone or another small device. A display lights up beneath the surface to show you the remaining power as a percentage, and the current charging rate. It’s nice and compact, with a generous 10,000-mAh battery capacity, and comes in black, white, green, or pink. Anker supplies stickers to stop your Apple Watch from sliding, but I didn’t find that to be a problem.

Industry observers note that innovative and genuinely useful, I love the Nimble SharePower, a 10,000-mAh, modular power bank that you can snap in half to get two separate, fully functional 5,000-mAh chargers. This clever design allows you to share power with friends and family. The two halves connect magnetically with tiny pogo pins (it’s satisfying to pull them apart and reconnect). One has a built-in USB-C cable that doubles as a carry loop, and the other has a fold-out USB-C connector. Put them together, and the remaining power is split evenly between the two halves. My daughter pinched this soon after it arrived in my home because it enables her to share the power with her friends, and I’m having trouble getting it back.

In a recent development, there are so many portable chargers out there. Here are a few more I like that just missed out on a place above for one reason or another. We also have separate guides for the Best Laptop Power Banks, Best MagSafe Power Banks, and Best Portable Power Stations.

With its lovely textured finish and sleek design, this magnetic Qi2 power bank is a looker. It sticks to the back of your phone and charges wirelessly at 15 watts, also doubling as a stand for travel, thanks to its sturdy aluminum kickstand. When you plug it in via USB-C, it supports 25-watt wireless charging for your phone and pass-through charging, so it charges the battery at the same time. It has four LEDs and a power button on the bottom edge. On the downside, it’s expensive and doesn't come with a cable or power adapter.

It has been revealed that super svelte, about the same size as a stack of credit cards, this charger slides easily into pockets and bags and offers a modest top-up for your phone. The USB-C connector pops out, and it comes in loads of colors.

How slim can a MagSafe power bank get? This one is just 0.27 inches, the thinnest I’ve tested, and it sticks to the back of your iPhone (or Qi2 Android phone) magnetically. It has two USB-C ports and one USB-A, is fast to recharge (around 90 minutes at 100 watts), supports most fast-charging protocols and trickle charging for small devices, and is CCC certified for trips to China.

Thoughtfully designed power banks with an IP67 rating, built-in shock absorbers, and screw-on caps for the ports.

This compact carbon fiber Nitecore power bank is the lightest I’ve tested with a 10,000-mAh capacity. The tradeoff to keep the weight down is that it’s relatively slow (no heat sink). You can expect a 15-watt charging rate, though it can recharge at up to 22.5 watts. These portable chargers I tested aren’t necessarily terrible, but you can do better.

UGreen MagFlow Pro for $90: I actually quite like this magnetic, wireless charging power bank (Qi2 25W) with its Matrix-style screen that animates to show charging status. But considering the 10,000-mAh capacity, the price is absolutely bonkers. The marketing talks up its cooling properties, but it got very warm when I used it. The attached USB-C cable (45W) was annoyingly obtrusive when it was stuck to the back of my iPhone.

OnePlus Slim Magnetic Power Bank for $70: Sleek in silver-gray aluminum with a chamfered edge, this power bank looks lovely, but the 5,000-mAh capacity is just over half that after inefficiency takes a bite.

It has been revealed that iniu Portable Charger for $20: It’s very small for a 10,000-mAh capacity. You can charge at up to 45 watts from either of the USB-C ports or 18 watts from the USB-A (recharging was slow), it fell short of the stated capacity, and the display sometimes failed to patch correctly.

FansDreams MChaos for $46: I love the idea of a wearable power bank, and this one comes in lime green with a carabiner that makes it easy to attach to a bag, but recharging is slow, and you’ll be lucky to get one full charge for your phone. It's also currently sold out.

iWalk Portable Charger for $22: The 4,800-mAh capacity won’t come close to fully refilling your device, but it's tiny enough to keep in a bag at all times.

What Features Should I Look for in Power Banks?

There are a few things worth thinking about when you’re shopping for a portable charger.

The capacity of a power bank is measured in milliampere-hours (mAh), but this can be a little misleading because the amount of power you get depends on the cable you use, the device you’re charging, and the charging method. (Qi wireless charging is less efficient.) You will never get the maximum capacity from any power bank. You can generally expect to get between 60 and 80 percent after energy loss through heat and conversion. Some manufacturers list a “Rated Capacity” that’s lower than the overall capacity to give you an indication of what to expect in real-world use. We try to provide a minimum estimate of what you’ll get in terms of charges for devices.

The charging rate for devices like smartphones is measured in watts (W), but most power banks list the voltage (V) and the amperage (A). Thankfully, you can calculate the wattage yourself simply by multiplying the voltage and amperage. Unfortunately, getting that maximum rate also depends on your device, the standards it supports, and the charging cable you use. Many smartphones, including Apple’s iPhones, support the power delivery standard, meaning you can use higher-power power banks to recharge the device with no concerns. A few phones, such as Samsung’s Galaxy S range, support a supplementary PD protocol called PPS (programmable power supply) that goes up to 45 watts. Many phones also support Qualcomm’s proprietary Quick Charge (QC) standard. There are also other proprietary fast-charging standards, but you won’t generally find power banks that support them unless they come from the smartphone manufacturer.

According to recent reports, your device will need pass-through support if you want to charge your power bank and use it to charge another device simultaneously. The Nimble, GoalZero, Biolite, Mophie, Zendure, and Sharge portable chargers listed support pass-through charging. Anker discontinued support for pass-through in some of its products because it found that differences between the output of the wall charger and the input of the device being charged can cause the power bank to cycle on and off rapidly and shorten its life. Monoprice does not support pass-through charging either. We would advise caution when using pass-through, as it can also cause portable chargers to heat up.

Can I Take a Power Bank on a Plane?

It’s safe to fly with a power bank, but there are two main restrictions to keep in mind when you board a flight: You must have the portable charger in your carry-on luggage (it cannot be checked), and it must not exceed 100 watt-hours. If your power bank has a larger capacity than 27,000 mAh, you should check with the airline. Below that should not be a problem.

Some airlines introduced stricter rules in 2025, so always check with your chosen airline before you travel. For example, some airlines prefer you not to use or charge power banks during a flight, some require power banks to be in your hand luggage under the seat in front of you and not in the overheads, and some limit the number of power banks you can have on board.

Why You Should Avoid Cheap Power Banks.

Many years ago, the Samsung Galaxy Note 7 gained notoriety when its batteries caught fire in a series of incidents. There’s been a steady stream of similar, though isolated, incidents ever since. Despite the high-profile coverage of batteries gone wrong, the vast majority of lithium-ion batteries are safe.

According to recent reports, the chemical reaction that occurs inside a lithium-ion cell is complex, but as in any battery, there’s a negative and a positive electrode. In lithium batteries, the negative is a lithium-carbon compound, and the positive is cobalt oxide (though many battery makers are moving away from cobalt). These two compounds cause a reaction that is safe when controlled and delivers energy to your devices. When the reaction gets out of control, though, you end up with earbuds melting in your ears. What changes a safe reaction to an uncontrolled reaction can be any number of things: excess heat, physical damage during use, physical damage during manufacture, or using the wrong charger.

The three basic rules that have kept me safe through testing dozens and dozens of batteries are these:.

Sources indicate that avoiding cheap wall-outlet adapters, cords, and chargers is the most crucial rule. These are your most likely sources of problems. Those chargers you see on Amazon for $20 cheaper than the competition? Not worth it. They probably got the price down by skimping on insulation, leaving out power-management tools, and ignoring the basics of electrical safety. Price alone is no guarantee of safety, either. Buy from reputable companies and brands.

Then there’s heat. Too much of it can cause all manner of problems, both in terms of discharge and safety. Avoid heat, and pay attention to your batteries when they’re charging. If your device gets overly hot when charging, this can be a sign of problems. Similarly, beware of any swollen, bulging, or otherwise misshapen batteries.

Why Is My Power Bank Charging Slowly?

Industry observers note that I’ve explained charging rates and capacity above, but several factors can cause charging speed to be slower than expected. The rate is determined by the device being charged, so your phone will request a certain wattage, which changes depending on how full its battery is, on-device settings, and the battery temperature.

All devices charge more slowly when they are completely empty, when the battery approaches full, and when they overheat. The cable you use will also have a maximum charging rate, and so will different ports on the power bank. Wireless charging is more convenient, but also slower than wired charging.

Sources indicate that I’ve been testing power banks for close to two decades, and my home office has stacks of ’em at any given moment. I test every portable charger that comes in for at least two weeks. I always check how many times it can fully charge my test phone (right now an iPhone 16). I’ll also try charging my Pixel 10 Pro XL and Samsung Galaxy S24+ to test charging speeds, and whatever else I have in. For larger-capacity power banks, I test-charge an iPad Mini and a MacBook Air. I test how long it takes to recharge each empty power bank.

Sources indicate that aside from these standard tests, I try to use the power banks in my everyday life, just to see how they feel, and my wife and kids often help out and share their opinions. For some of our top picks, I continue to test over months to get a sense of their reliability and durability, though it’s not possible to do this for every device that lands on my desk. Beyond function, I take form and usability into account. I keep an eye on user reviews and consider the warranties and customer service of each manufacturer.

How Does WIRED Select Power Banks to be Reviewed?

In a recent development, I often scan the latest releases to seek out worthy prospects, whether from an unknown new brand or an established favorite like Anker. I also get pitched many power banks every week. I sometimes reach out to those companies to ask for the product but never promise any kind of editorial coverage—that would go against WIRED’s editorial policies. While WIRED usually earns affiliate revenue if you purchase a power bank using our link, this is not factored into the decision on ranking.

There are too many power banks for me to test everything, so I tend to stick to known, reputable brands, but there’s always room for something new if it has a compelling new feature or price, and I cover as many as I can. (Leave a comment or send me an email if you want me to test a power bank from a certain brand!) Once testing is complete, I typically donate power banks to a local charity. I try to hang on to some of our top picks for comparison purposes and to test their longevity.

Breaking: How to block a device from your home network

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that it's easy to get rattled when you see a newly introduced, strange device connect to your network for the first time.
  • Industry observers note that start with your router's app.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Lock down a home network by tracking down MAC addresses, tweaking your router’s access controls and kicking unwanted users off your Wi-Fi.

Recent findings suggest that it's easy to get rattled when you see a newly introduced, strange device connect to your network for the first time. Most gateways and routers, provided by your ISP or purchased separately, come with companion apps that send you notifications when new devices connect to your network. Unfortunately, those new devices aren't always properly identified. For instance, a friend may connect with an Android device, (and if they are having trouble, you can suggest they clear their Android cache) but your app may identify it as a string of letters and numbers, or just "unknown." Not very helpful. This is because of safety and privacy features on the connecting devices, but how are you supposed to know what it is and when to block it from your network?

Industry observers note that start with your router's app. Keep in mind that every app is different, so there's no universal method for walking you through this. Look for terms like "connected devices" or "attached devices" to open a list of all connected, recently connected and unknown devices. If you jump on a PC and use the browser, your ISP's instructions or the manual for your router and modem/gateway (or learning the difference between a router, modem, and gateway) will help walk you through it. You'll need the administrative login as well, but it may be different from the password you regularly use to join Wi-Fi.

Sources indicate that don't just start blocking anything and everything. Look at the MAC address on each connected device, then match it to the MAC address on the devices in your home. Most Androids and iPhones will let you access the Wi-Fi/MAC address in the Settings. On an iPhone, access Settings > Wi-Fi Network > Wi-Fi Address. On most Androids, access Settings > About Device > Status Information or Hardware Information.

Industry observers note that when you find an out-of-place device on the list and determine that it's not yours, open its entry in your router's app and look for an option to block. Depending on the router, it might be under "Access Control," "MAC Filtering" or something along those lines. Follow the instructions for your router or gateway model. On a Netgear router, for instance, controls are under Advanced, Security and Access Control.Make sure you enable the feature and select the device you want to block or remove. Just make sure you don't accidentally block the device you're using for access. That'll be a fun little puzzle to unravel.

Sources indicate that always read what each setting does. Pausing is not the same as removing or blocking. Removing doesn't necessarily mean the device can't reconnect. If you want to block a device, you need to block it for certain. Of course, a strange device connected to your Wi-Fi is a strong indicator that someone knows your password. Naturally, that needs to change. Pronto. If a neighbor is accessing your network without your permission, blocking their device won't solve the problem because they can simply access it again with another device.

In a recent development, the faster you change the password — or consider whether a passkey vs password is better — the better. Create and save a new and very unique password for your Wi-Fi network. If you need more ways to secure yourself, there are other steps you can take right now to be safer online.

Writing your Wi-Fi password down is often discouraged, which is entirely understandable. But if that's the best way you have of remembering it, place the password somewhere safe, where nobody can find it but you and your family. Please don't tape it to your router or your computer screen.

Once you've removed every unwanted device from your network and changed your password, you need to avoid the common mistakes to avoid when setting up a home network to turn it into a fortress. You need more than a unique password for your Wi-Fi access. Change the administrator password that protects your router's settings too. Changing your Wi-Fi password has no effect on the administrator password, so both need a fresh start. Next, dig into your router's wireless security settings. If your equipment supports it, use WPA3 Personal or WPA2 Personal. WEP and WPA are outdated. Make sure your router's firmware is up-to-date and that automatic updates are enabled. If your model is getting a little long in the tooth and is no longer supported, it's time for an upgrade.

For visitors and vacationing family members, set up a guest network with its own unique password. That way, you don't have to hand out your own and run the risk of your password access spreading. Review the connected device list now and then. You don't have to look at it daily, but it's a good idea to keep an eye on it so you can catch any new and unexpected additions. Some apps will let you rename the devices. Take the time to do so, and you'll always know what is what.

According to recent reports, last but not least, turn off SSID broadcasting. You can hide your network name, so your neighbor or whoever is intruding on your home network can't see it on their Wi-Fi list. To connect latest devices, you'll need to manually type in your network name. Intruders can spoof SSIDs and, with network scanners, find a hidden SSID. Which is why you should stay vigilant and check your app often. Make sure any new traffic is legitimate.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, it’s now been 21 years since I first published an article at Ars Technica. It has been the only home I’ve known as a writer, and it has been essential to my development from scientist to blogger to journalist. It’s no exaggeration to say that Ars has helped make me who I am today.

So, asking you to support Ars via a subscription is very personal (and a bit selfish) for me—I’d like to stay here! Jobs that give you this sort of independence, that let you both edit and write, are very rare in journalism, and I’m unlikely to find another. Helping secure Ars’ future through your support will mean I don’t have to.

Sources indicate that but I’d rather make a case for why you’ll benefit from supporting Ars. In fact, I’ll make three: the writing, the people, and the community.

It has been revealed that since my start here, the central mission of Ars has been the same: cover the news in a way that helps our readers understand the facts and why they’re notable. The landscape has shifted dramatically over that time—technology, science, and policy are very different from 21 years ago. But understanding those changes and why they happened matters. It matters for everything from what you should buy today to what the world you’re going to be living in 10 years from now will look like.

I’ve had the privilege of helping to decide how to translate that mission to science coverage. That decision took place against an notable backdrop: While most people value things like evidence and research, they often struggle to recognize how those are used to build a body of reliable scientific information. That struggle kind of made the decision for me. Putting people in the know means helping them understand how science works as a process, and why that can produce information about the world we can trust.

Recent findings suggest that focusing on that has made our science coverage different from most of what you can get elsewhere. We don’t just tell you what’s newly introduced in the world of science; we help you understand the history of the significant questions, the breakthroughs that allow us to address old problems in new ways, and the clever ideas people have for how to extract reliable information from a noisy and chaotic Universe. I’d like to think our readers get more out of that sort of writing, and it’s worth supporting.

Sources indicate that but I’d be giving you a very incomplete picture of things if I only talked about science. Everyone at Ars has had to think about what sort of stories and presentation fit best with our mission. While our writing is essential now, it’s the people behind it that will ensure that it remains vital no matter what other changes come our way in the coming decades. And I can say with more than a little confidence that Ars is full of people you can trust to keep it that way.

Recent findings suggest that one reason you can trust that is that the people at Ars now are, in many cases, the same ones who were here when you first started reading the site. We have remarkably low turnover, especially at the higher levels in our organization. There are two reasons for that: Ars is incredibly well-managed, and the people here believe in our mission.

The former is important because it should assure you that the money we get from your subscription won’t be wasted on some ill-advised pivot to video, or whatever the next craze is. The latter matters because it’s the people here who make Ars what it is. I work with some of the most thoughtful people I have ever encountered, and they all care deeply about making our work informative and compelling. I have also been lucky enough to work with a large group of freelancers over the years, and I have nothing but good things to say about them. We work hard to make sure that, even when the name on the byline is unfamiliar to you, you can be confident that you’re getting the same quality of reporting.

All of them—the full-time staff and the freelancers—are smart, great writers and know their areas of expertise better than most people in this business. Like I’m sure you do, I learn a lot from what they write (unlike you, I also get the bonus of learning from them in our Slack channels).

In a recent development, but it’s not just my fellow writers whom I’ve learned from. We’ve got one of the smartest communities on the Internet, with experts from pretty much every area we cover regularly contributing to the comments. In the discussions attached to my articles, I have regularly seen them fill in details I didn’t have space to mention, clarify things in response to other readers’ questions, and talk about related topics that didn’t really fit into the article. I’ve learned a lot from this, and I’m confident the rest of the readers have, too.

It has been revealed that it’s strange to say the opposite of one of the central dogmas of the Internet: Read the comments. But it’s something I’ve told our freelance writers pretty regularly.

Sources indicate that we’ve kept things that way even as most other sites’ comments turned toxic and were shut off. That’s taken both an editorial commitment and lots of staff time spent moderating and engaging in community management. Those don’t come for free, so your subscriptions will help support that, too.

Industry observers note that I hope you’ll consider signing up if you’re able. Beyond the financials, I know we all appreciate it as a sign we’re on the right track.

#70316. ‘So what if there’s a hole? It hasn’t collapsed’: Kyiv residents unbothered by Russian attacks on city’s bridges

‘So what if there’s a hole? It hasn’t collapsed’: Kyiv residents unbothered by Russian attacks on city’s bridges

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1000 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theguardian

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Despite dodging tears in the tarmac, people are confident in city’s infrastructure – and will not worry about what has not happened yet.
  • Mykola expects to drive his battered beige passenger minibus 20 to 24 times a day past the holes in the road on Kyiv’s damaged Northern Bridge that were caused by a Russian ballistic missile attack on Tuesday.
  • Buses are now the only motor transport allowed across the normally busy multi-lane crossing, though on their way into the city centre they have to skirt the tears in the tarmac, using the only functioning lane to get by.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Despite dodging tears in the tarmac, people are confident in city’s infrastructure – and will not worry about what has not happened yet.

Mykola expects to drive his battered beige passenger minibus 20 to 24 times a day past the holes in the road on Kyiv’s damaged Northern Bridge that were caused by a Russian ballistic missile attack on Tuesday.

Buses are now the only motor transport allowed across the normally busy multi-lane crossing, though on their way into the city centre they have to skirt the tears in the tarmac, using the only functioning lane to get by.

“So what if there’s a hole? The bridge hasn’t collapsed. You need to know a bit about bridge construction,” states Mykola, 65, at the wheel of a half -full afternoon bus as it clatters on its way west.

Mykola operates a marshrutka, a single deck private bus, whose drivers are famed in Kyiv mythology for being able to multi-task: chatting, smoking and collecting fares, while driving as fast as possible to take passengers from rivals.

Passengers pay 25 hryvnia (42p) in cash and typically one passenger gets the unofficial job of taking money and handing back change on behalf of the driver. It turns out this has become the Guardian’s task, in order to conduct an interview.

It has been revealed that “It would be very difficult to destroy the bridge. It would take a huge number of missiles, and if one or two hit it, it wouldn’t be the end of the world,” Mykola continues, with behind-the-wheel speculation that is so far accurate. By lunchtime the holes have been covered up, perhaps to avoid unsettling passengers eyeing the Dnipro River below.

Alongside its attacks on the capital’s electricity, heating and water systems, Russia has been attacking Kyiv’s bridges since early October, trying to cut off the city centre in the west from the newer, largely residential east, home to about a third of its population.

Moscow struck the bridges twice again this week, first on Tuesday – overshadowed by Ukraine’s partial destruction of the Kerch road bridge to Crimea. Then again during a noisy Thursday night, hours after Vladimir Putin promised there would be a “far more painful” response to the demolition of his pet project.

According to recent reports, as of Friday, in an already traffic-snarled city, Kyiv’s other main road bridge, the Southern Bridge, was allowing motor traffic only from east to west. The fresh Podilskyi Bridge, damaged early on Friday, was similarly restricted, and the city’s mayor, Vitali Klitschko, told people to avoid car travel after a night in which six were killed.

The Northern Bridge remains open for public transport – plus any cyclists, scooter riders and walkers willing to brave the damp late autumn weather and ignore missile and drone alerts. But below, earthworks have begun to prepare for a floating pontoon bridge, one of eight planned, in case of the worst.

It has been revealed that dmytro Bespalov, a transport planning expert with Kyiv’s National University of Construction and Architecture, said it was difficult to destroy a suspension bridge like the Northern. They have “a strong construction, with a lot of repairability”, meaning damage can usually be fixed. Though there are holes in the roadway, its supporting structures were so far unscathed, he added.

Russia is thought to have been aiming ballistic missiles at the supporting pylon, requiring a precise and difficult to execute attack, though that is what Ukraine did at the culmination of its complex attack on the Kerch road bridge, which was brought down after a Flamingo cruise missile struck its supporting arch.

Yet, Bespalov cautioned that Kyiv was strategically vulnerable if Russia targets the bridges with “dozens or hundreds” of missiles, because the city did not have enough bridges from before the war. “In 2021, Kyiv was in third place in Europe for congestion on the TomTom traffic index,” he said, behind Istanbul and Moscow.

Particular concern is reserved for the pontoon bridge alternative. They can bear less traffic: “It would take 20 pontoon bridges to have half the current capacity,” Bespalov said – and they are far more vulnerable to missile and drone attack. “I don’t think it would be possible to use pontoons during a red [missile] or yellow [drone] alarm” – not least because vehicles could end up in the water.

At the first busy bus stop on the eastern left bank, Nataliya, 40, and Iryna, 39, are happy to make the crossing over the Northern Bridge. They say they have long got used to the difficulties of war: “The main thing is to get through the first 24 hours at home after the initial discomfort, and then we’ll adapt,” remarked Nataliya, a customer service specialist.

Iryna added: “If we start to despair, that’s exactly what they want. A bridge can be built. The main thing is that when the attack comes, there are no civilians or military personnel around. It’s just concrete, that’s all. They’ll either repair it or come up with something latest.”.

It is a core attitude of Kyiv’s remaining residents, who are already contending with hours of electricity shortages and a lack of heating, with the full chill of winter yet to arrive. People want to deal with problems as they arise rather than worrying excessively about what may come – though it is not always easy amid the daily attacks, including a daytime raid on Thursday in which a drone exploded near the Dutch embassy.

Sources indicate that oleksandr, 42, a construction worker, was waiting to get across the bridge. “If the bridges are destroyed we’ll have to leave,” he conceded. If that happened, he and his wife would move to her parents’ house across the river. “I bought them a generator there; they have their own water well. We’d already dug the well during the war. They used to have gas heating, but we’ve converted it to wood-burning. We’re preparing,” he said.

Additional reporting by Galya Rudyk.

#70315. Why Apple Vision Pro never took off like Meta's VR headsets

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (876 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Engadget ↗ Open Full Page

Why Apple Vision Pro never took off like Meta's VR headsets

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (876 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Good hardware doesn't necessarily make for a successful product.
  • Sources indicate that when Apple introduced the Vision Pro headset in early 2024, it was the most ambitious device the tech colossus had released in recent memory.
  • It has been revealed that but from our vantage point in 2026, it's clear the Vision Pro was doomed from the start.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Good hardware doesn't necessarily make for a successful product.

Sources indicate that when Apple introduced the Vision Pro headset in early 2024, it was the most ambitious device the tech colossus had released in recent memory. To find another device that so fundamentally wanted to change how we use tech, you'd probably have to go back to the original iPhone.

It has been revealed that but from our vantage point in 2026, it's clear the Vision Pro was doomed from the start. Despite its extraordinary capabilities, design flaws and a lack of apps at launch held it back significantly. But perhaps most damaging of all was its price. For $3,500, you'd expect the Vision Pro to do everything your MacBook does and more, but for many consumers, it became a glorified and overcomplicated external monitor. After an initial wave of hype, the Vision Pro faded away.

According to recent reports, the Vision Pro got a single, half-hearted M5 upgrade in October 2025, but the writing was on the wall. Apple was already pulling staff from the project to focus on cheaper, more approachable smart glasses and, by June 2026, analyst Ming-Chi Kuo suggested that Apple had dropped its headset program entirely, leaving only a couple of smart glasses in development.

In a recent development, but other VR and XR headsets have fared better, most notably the Meta Quest 2, which became the best-selling VR headset of all time, and its successor, the Quest 3. Why did Meta succeed enough to remain in the market while Apple failed despite releasing a polished first-generation product? The answer is twofold: Apple doesn't need the Vision Pro as much as Meta needed the Quest, and the Vision Pro sacrificed mainstream accessibility to meet Apple's notoriously rigid product standards.

In a recent development, when the Apple Vision Pro arrived, some analysts were astounded by its $3,500 price, a number that suggests Apple never intended it to become truly mainstream. Apple might be able to get away with charging $1,000 for an iPhone or $2,000 for an iPhone Duo (especially with carrier subsidies, deals and purchase plans), but more than triple that for a device that required consumers not only to learn an entirely new operating system in three dimensions but also to find a practical use for it in their daily lives? It was never going to tempt anyone beyond the wealthiest subset of Apple enthusiasts, especially since it lacked any killer apps at launch.

More charitable onlookers insisted Apple had a larger vision for the Vision Pro. The first generation was for developers, some said, and mass appeal would materialize as future headsets got cheaper and added more apps. But a classic chicken-and-egg problem emerged: no one wanted to develop for a platform with so few consumers, and few users wanted to buy into a platform with so few native apps. It's a tale as old as time, with products like the Windows Phone and Apple's own Newton PDA falling victim to the same dilemma.

Sources indicate that while Apple hasn't released concrete sales data for the Vision Pro, estimates generally put the figure at around or under 500,000 units. That's far below Apple's initial expectations and less than what such a complex, cutting-edge device would need to sell to make financial sense. Demand for a device that costs more than your mortgage payment and makes you look like you're wearing the world's dorkiest ski goggles was, as it turns out, not very high.

Despite the Meta Quest line's relative success, it hasn't really made VR and XR that popular. While the Quest 2 is widely considered the best-selling VR headset of all time, even the most generous estimates put sales at around 20 million units. By way of comparison, the Sony PlayStation 4 sold more than 100 million units, and Apple sold around 226 million iPhones in 2024 alone. Compared to sales numbers for popular tech products, VR's best-selling product barely registers. Its follow-up, the Quest 3, was even less impressive, only unseating the Quest 2 as the most popular headset on Steam in late 2026.

The Quest 2's figures can't be fully chalked up to consumer enthusiasm, either. Facebook poured over $80 billion into the so-called metaverse starting in 2021, even renaming itself to Meta as part of its effort to dominate what Mark Zuckerberg called the "next chapter for the internet." The Quest 2 was Meta's flagship headset at the time, so it makes sense it got more attention than other VR headsets. For his part, Zuckerberg could not have been more wrong and, while Meta has seen success with its AI-equipped Meta glasses, it has failed to move the needle on full-fat VR and XR headsets.

One warning sign for Apple in the lead-up to the Vision Pro's release should have been Meta's own high-end headset, the Quest Pro. Launched in October 2022 for $1,500, the Quest Pro promised everything Meta couldn't afford to put in its budget-priced Quest 2: eye tracking, productivity software and better passthrough. It was an immediate flop, prompting Meta to slash $500 off the price about six months later before discontinuing it in 2024. In that context, it's no wonder Apple's $3,500 headset didn't fare much better.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Just how happy is Rockstar Games with the sales performance of its long-awaited Grand Theft Auto VI? Here's a clue: it didn't even wait 48 hours before releasing the first-day sales figures. According to its official statement, GTA VI's "day one retail sales reached $3.79 billion, setting a new record for entertainment across any medium, and becoming the biggest entertainment launch in history.".

Included in that tally is revenue from an astonishing 32.5 million preorders, making it the most pre-ordered game in history on both Xbox and PlayStation, according to Microsoft, makers of the Xbox game console and Sony, makers of the Playstation, the only two systems that can at the moment play the game.

But it's when you put those numbers into perspective that you get a sense of how astonishingly successful Rockstar's launch truly was. Spider-Man: Brand Latest Day is the highest-grossing movie of 2026, according to Box Office Mojo, with worldwide ticket sales exceeding $2.5 billion. That film was released at the end of July, more than three months ago, but Grand Theft Auto VI has already exceeded its worldwide box office total by more than a billion dollars.

But what if we widened our search? On Box Office Mojo's ranking of the highest-grossing movies of all time, 2019's Avengers: Endgame ranks near the top with worldwide ticket sales of over $2.9 billion — still well short of Rockstar's GTA VI score.

Rockstar's co-founder and current president Sam Houser was understandably elated by the reception to his manufacturer's magnum opus: "It is with immense gratitude that we enter a fresh chapter of Rockstar Games with the release of Grand Theft Auto VI. We are incredibly humbled by the response from players around the world and we couldn’t be more excited to share this moment with you.".

But the good news likely doesn't end there. Rockstar Games and parent organization Take-Two Interactive have at least two more major paydays to look forward to: the release of Grand Theft Auto VI on the multiplayer platform GTA Online and the future PC port, which would give PC players a chance to buy the game. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • All options open in future talks, says Ed Miliband, while prime minister hails ‘a good day for Britain and Europe’.
  • The UK rejoining the EU could be on the table in informal discussions between Andy Burnham and European leaders in Brussels, Ed Miliband has noted.
  • The foreign secretary mentioned “all options” would be examined in the process, after the prime minister agreed deals on trade and young people with the bloc on Friday.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

All options open in future talks, says Ed Miliband, while prime minister hails ‘a good day for Britain and Europe’.

The UK rejoining the EU could be on the table in informal discussions between Andy Burnham and European leaders in Brussels, Ed Miliband has noted.

The foreign secretary mentioned “all options” would be examined in the process, after the prime minister agreed deals on trade and young people with the bloc on Friday.

Agreements on food and drink standards, emissions trading and a youth mobility scheme were revealed after talks this week. Under the plans, 100,000 young Britons will be allowed to live, work, study and travel in the EU, with similar access for Europeans in the UK.

Burnham said the agreement would add 0.5% to the UK’s GDP, a £17bn boost to the British economy.

Sources indicate that miliband mentioned Burnham would have further “brainstorming” discussions with the EU in the next year about what could happen next. He said the agreements this week were the limit of what could be done before the next general election.

However, the trio of deals could be derailed in six months, as the EU threatened to block them unless the UK allows European students to pay domestic-level fees to study at British universities.

Miliband noted in an interview for the BBC’s Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg that “all the options will be on the table” when pressed on whether rejoining the bloc would be considered, adding: “We will look at the benefits and the costs of all the different options.”.

In a recent development, since entering government in 2024, Labour has stuck to the “red lines” in its manifesto, which stated the party would not rejoin the single market or customs union. It also ruled out freedom of movement.

Burnham has previously said he wants to see the UK rejoin the EU in his lifetime.

In a recent development, the prime minister will use the announcement of his 10-year plan before Christmas to explore how the UK could get closer to the EU after the next election. Informal discussions will take place with Brussels before next year’s UK-EU summit.

Miliband said he accepts the result of the 2016 vote but “the world has changed massively”.

In a recent development, “Europe is changing too, so we’ve got to look at what that means,” he mentioned. “It’s not about this parliament, we’re respecting the red lines in this parliament.”.

Sources indicate that he also denied the deal with the EU would rely on progress in discussions on students from the bloc coming to the UK. It has been reported that a proposal from the bloc to lower the level of tuition fees paid by EU students in the UK has not been agreed.

Miliband told the BBC it was “absolutely clear” the agreements on food exports, energy and youth mobility would apply, even though there has not been a deal on tuition fees.

The foreign secretary said: “The dates are set out in 2028 when these things are coming in, we’re introducing legislation in parliament, so definitely.”.

It has been revealed that on Friday, Burnham stated the agreement represented a “good day for Britain and Europe”. He said the agreements answer “the biggest challenges of our times and the biggest worries that people have”, citing the cost of living, lack of economic growth, illegal immigration and challenges facing young people.

Recent findings suggest that “The deal is done. It is there in black and white in front of you,” Burnham mentioned, adding that the legislation would enter parliament next week.

The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, played down the disagreement, saying she was “confident we are going to find a solution”. About the further discussions, she mentioned: “We welcome this brainstorming, so count on us.”.

Recent findings suggest that the environment secretary, Angela Eagle, told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme on Saturday the deal was good for farmers. “(It) will open up new markets. They’ll be able to import and expor. This is a win-win for the UK. We will dissolve a lot of the friction and costs at the border for UK agriculture and food.”.

Breaking: Only the Seminole Tribe can offer online gambling in Florida—and they're furious at DraftKings

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Last week, DraftKings asked a federal court in Florida to take over a lawsuit recently filed against it by the Seminole Tribe, opening another front in the nationwide online “swaps” debate.
  • This Florida case adds to an already complex subplot involving Indigenous tribes, some of which are challenging prediction markets, while others are trying to get in on the action themselves.
  • In the new lawsuit, the Seminole Tribe contends that two of DraftKings’ current online offerings—the fantasy sports-style “Pick6” and the “Super App” sportsbook—are “illegal” in Florida.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Last week, DraftKings asked a federal court in Florida to take over a lawsuit recently filed against it by the Seminole Tribe, opening another front in the nationwide online “swaps” debate.

This Florida case adds to an already complex subplot involving Indigenous tribes, some of which are challenging prediction markets, while others are trying to get in on the action themselves.

In the new lawsuit, the Seminole Tribe contends that two of DraftKings’ current online offerings—the fantasy sports-style “Pick6” and the “Super App” sportsbook—are “illegal” in Florida.

The tribe argues that every such “wager that Defendants now accept through their illegal sportsbook siphons away revenue that funds both the Tribe’s and Florida’s public programs and government services.”.

Neither DraftKings nor its attorneys immediately responded to Ars’ request for comment. However, in a court filing, DraftKings indicates that its products available to Floridians are merely “fantasy sports and the trading of [financial] derivatives” and not gambling.

DraftKings notes that its “licensed sportsbook” operates in other states but “not in Florida.”.

Multiple companies, including DraftKings, claim that their “swaps” (a type of financial derivative) are, in fact, properly governed by a federal agency, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission. Therefore, DraftKings argues, states cannot regulate this activity as gambling.

Sources indicate that the Seminoles, a sovereign nation and a federally recognized tribe, have a deal with the State of Florida, known as the 2021 Gaming Compact. That 30-year contract allows the tribe to maintain what the tribe states is the “exclusive right to offer online sports betting throughout the State of Florida.” In exchange, this betting regime is regulated, and Florida takes a cut.

But since that contract was signed, attorneys for the Seminole Tribe say in the complaint, DraftKings has pursued years of court challenges and a failed ballot measure designed to break into the Sunshine State.

As of 2026, DraftKings rolled out “Pick6” in Florida, a game where individuals can put money down while predicting specific outcomes—for example, whether Victor Wembanyama of the San Antonio Spurs will score more or less than 28.5 points in his next basketball game.

Recent findings suggest that “Based on DraftKings’ representations, Florida consumers may predictably but incorrectly conclude that Pick6 is a legal product in Florida. It is not,” the complaint states.

“Pick6 is illegal ‘gambling’ under Florida law. DraftKings operates Pick6 without a license, without state oversight, and without any consumer protections Florida requires as a condition of legal sports wagering.”.

In June 2026, DraftKings rolled out what it calls a “Super App,” which the Seminole Tribe argues is a “one-stop shop for illegal gambling,” as it provides an interface that is “in the same format used by every traditional, regulated sportsbook.”.

Florida-based professor Robert Jarvis of Nova Southeastern University studies gambling law, and he told Ars by email that he didn’t “buy the argument” DraftKings put forward that its products cannot be regulated under Florida gambling law.

Jarvis also noted that the tribe caught a break, too, with their randomly assigned federal judge.

“Not only have they had very good luck in federal court in previous cases, the federal judge assigned to the case is Ed Artau, who previously served as a Florida state trial judge (2014–20) and a Florida state appellate judge (2020–25),” he wrote. “Thus, in a sense, the Seminoles get the best of both worlds: a federal court run by a Florida state judge.”.

Workers of the Indian Youth Congress (IYC), the youth wing of the opposition Indian National Congress, protested at US tech giant Meta's offices in Hyderabad, Mumbai and Gurugram on Friday, demanding that the group's leaders' Instagram accounts be restored.

In Hyderabad, protesters entered the building, smashed plants and clashed with police, according to footage the IYC released. Meta declined to comment.

The IYC stated Instagram withheld the accounts of its president and in-charge on November 19 "on BJP orders," referring to the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party, and restored both shortly after the protests.
