    Tech Report: SpaceX lenders don’t want Elon Musk launching their collateral into space

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (519 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Lenders backing SpaceX’s latest $43 billion debt package, which is secured by its advanced AI chips, have tried to bar Elon Musk from firing the collateral into space as part of his plan for orbital data centers.
    • Industry observers note that the world’s richest man has outlined ambitious prepares to power AI models with data centers cooled by the vacuum of space.
    • According to recent reports, spaceX has remarked it plans to use the chips involved in the debt deal on Earth.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Lenders backing SpaceX’s latest $43 billion debt package, which is secured by its advanced AI chips, have tried to bar Elon Musk from firing the collateral into space as part of his plan for orbital data centers.

    Industry observers note that the world’s richest man has outlined ambitious prepares to power AI models with data centers cooled by the vacuum of space. That will require packing satellites full of advanced chips.

    According to recent reports, spaceX has remarked it plans to use the chips involved in the debt deal on Earth. But lenders have expressed concerns that if the group later decided to shoot the valuable chips that underpin their loans into space, it would prevent them from reclaiming and selling the semiconductors in the event of a default, according to people familiar with the matter.

    It is uncertain whether the provision was included in the finalized documents.

    The bonds were issued by a special purpose vehicle designed to keep the debt off SpaceX’s balance sheet and preserve its investment-grade credit rating.

    The proposed debt covenant presented potential legal challenges for SpaceX’s ambitions to build data centers in space, highlighting the uncharted territory that investors need to navigate when financing the nascent asset class.

    SpaceX sold more than $30 billion of the debt to large investors on Thursday as part of a financing package dubbed “Project Saturn.” The largest portion of the debt package was a $25 billion investment-grade bond backed by SpaceX’s five-year lease payment for the Nvidia chips.

    The debt was sold at 3.45 percentage points above US Treasuries, indicating a total yield of about 8.3 percent, the people said. SpaceX’s corporate debt maturing in 2031, meanwhile, traded at a yield of about 7.2 percent on Thursday.

    The newest bonds will mature in 2032, but the principal will be paid off in less than four years—an arrangement that was designed to reduce credit risks for lenders, the people added.

    More than $19 billion of the bonds already secured commitments prior to Thursday, including $4 billion from Pimco.

    Sources indicate that apollo and Goldman Sachs, which led the transaction, declined to comment. Pimco declined to comment. SpaceX did not respond to a request for comment.

    Funds managed and advised by BlackRock, Goldman Sachs Asset Management, and KKR have also made anchor commitments in the transaction, according to SpaceX.

    SpaceX plans to use the chips in US data centers majority-owned, controlled, and operated by SpaceX, according to a rating report issued by Moody’s.

    Sources indicate that moody’s assigned the debt an A3 rating, one notch above SpaceX’s own credit rating. KBRA rated the debt A-minus.

    The credit rating agencies attributed the A-tier rating in part to “hell-or-high-water” clauses that prevent SpaceX from walking away from the lease.

    “The SpaceX GPU deal appears cleverly structured and should appeal to a panoply of buyers, potentially including deep pools of insurance capital seeking attractive yield on investment-grade debt,” noted Grant Nachman, chief investment officer at Shorecliff Asset Management.

    “This transaction could prove a harbinger of future issuances,” he remarked.

    Additional reporting by Jill R Shah in Latest York.

    #70279. How to easily factory reset your Fitbit

    How to easily factory reset your Fitbit

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (715 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It can help fix a serious problem or prep your wearable for a newly introduced owner.
    • In a recent development, if your Fitbit is acting up, you'll want to restart it, but this is a very different process from a factory reset.
    • There are only a few times you'll want to factory reset a Fitbit.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It can help fix a serious problem or prep your wearable for a newly introduced owner.

    In a recent development, if your Fitbit is acting up, you'll want to restart it, but this is a very different process from a factory reset. You may want to restart your Fitbit if it won't sync with the Google Health app or isn't registering data. However, if the screen is unresponsive to taps or swipes, or it's frozen on a specific screen, you can force a hard restart, which typically involves pressing and holding a button (or buttons) for a specific period of time until the screen resets. How to restart your Fitbit device varies by model. It's a refresh, like turning something off and on again. A factory reset, on the other hand, removes all unsynced settings and data from the device and brings the wearable back to its original state when it was first purchased.

    There are only a few times you'll want to factory reset a Fitbit. Do this if you're giving it to someone else or selling it. It's also worth doing for data privacy, if the device is no longer functioning properly and you're dropping it off for safe recycling. Finally, it's a last-ditch effort if a restart isn't fixing a major issue. Factory resetting your Fitbit is simple, but use this option only when necessary.

    For Fitbits with a screen, go to Settings > About > Device Info > Clear User Data or Factory Reset. You may need to hold down a button on the screen to confirm, and you should feel a slight vibration when it's done and the Fitbit logo reappears on-screen. With the newest Fitbit Edge, it's even easier: swipe down from the top of the screen and select Settings > Clear User Data.

    It has been revealed that with older Fitbit trackers, you may have to connect the device to its charger and hold down a button or use a paperclip. With the Fitbit Flex, for example, which does not have a screen, connect the sensor to its charger, plug the charger into your computer via USB, find the black reset hole, and press it for three seconds with a paperclip. Wait for it to light up and confirm the reset.

    Recent findings suggest that interestingly, the upcoming screenless Fitbit Air (see our Fitbit Air review) does not have a traditional factory reset option. Instead, place it on its charger and press and hold the back button for 10 seconds (or until the status light flashes white). This will restart the device. If a new user pairs with the wearable, your account data will be cleared automatically.

    It's a good idea to manually unpair a Fitbit Air from your account first if you're handing it off. In the app, select the device from the top-left corner and, under System, select Disconnect & reset device. If it's not connecting to a new phone, forget it from your phone's Bluetooth menu (Settings > Bluetooth > tap the "i" beside the device and select Forget This Device.

    Industry observers note that A factory reset is a last-resort option. I recently had problems syncing my Fitbit Edge with my iPhone; it got stuck in a boot loop and froze on a specific screen. Nothing I tried worked until I tried a factory reset.

    Recent findings suggest that it's important to reiterate that a factory reset will erase all data that is stored locally on the device. This could include morning alarms, goals, notification settings, and any unsynced activities. It does not, however, delete data that's already been synced to the Google Health app. After resetting my Fitbit Edge, for example, all my daily data, including steps, workouts, and more, were still accessible in the app.

    According to recent reports, if you're holding onto an older, discontinued Fitbit model and it's still working, look for instructions on how to factory reset it in the supporting documentation online, or check the Help menu in the Google Health app. Whichever model you have, once the factory reset process is done, it's like a upcoming device again, and you can start the pairing and syncing process from scratch. Be patient: It may take some time to start accurately tracking your data again.

    US will soon announce root cause behind FAA nationwide ground stop

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 25 min read (5006 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

    ⏱️ ~25 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The US government will announce soon the root cause of the router outage that led to the third-ever nationwide ground stop issued by the US Federal Aviation Administration.
    • The nationwide ground stop blocked flight departures and impacted more than 1 million passengers across the United States for more than four hours on Friday, November 13.
    • It has been revealed that nearly one week later, FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford told news reporters that government investigators are “very close” to figuring out the root cause of the nationwide ground stop, according to CNN.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The US government will announce soon the root cause of the router outage that led to the third-ever nationwide ground stop issued by the US Federal Aviation Administration. But questions remain about whether the FAA’s effort to modernize the national airspace system is being done with all the proper risk assessments and adequate agency oversight of the private contractors involved.

    The nationwide ground stop blocked flight departures and impacted more than 1 million passengers across the United States for more than four hours on Friday, November 13. More than 12,000 flights were canceled on that day alone, with the number rising to more than 20,000 over the weekend as stranded travelers scrambled to find accommodations or alternative transportation. Some international flights were allowed to depart prior to the broader resumption of air traffic.

    It has been revealed that nearly one week later, FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford told news reporters that government investigators are “very close” to figuring out the root cause of the nationwide ground stop, according to CNN. Bedford also remarked that Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy aims to announce the findings at a news conference as soon as Friday, November 20.

    According to recent reports, problems first arose when “data began flooding” the FAA Telecommunications Infrastructure (FTI) network with 1,000 connection attempts every 4 to 5 seconds, according to an FAA Q&A post on November 15. The FTI network supports the flow of crucial flight data along with voice and video communications to air traffic control centers across the country.

    That caused “instability with aircraft communications and radar feeds” at 17 of the 22 Air Route Traffic Control Centers that manage en-route air traffic across the country, according to the FAA. The instability also impacted several Terminal Radar Approach Control facilities that guide aircraft both on approach and when departing from airports.

    An initial agency investigation identified a radar site in Amarillo, Texas, and a radio communications site in El Dorado, Arkansas, as “the reason for the excessive data flooding the systems.” The FAA’s network service provider, L3Harris, was installing a fresh router at the El Dorado site when the incident occurred and had recently installed a similar router in Texas.

    Recent findings suggest that specifically, the L3Harris contractor was deploying a new Juniper Networks router to replace a 25-year-old Cisco router at the El Dorado site. But the subsequent incident prompted the FAA to pause installation of the Juniper routers and turn off those that had already been installed, falling back on the older Cisco routers, according to the Associated Press.

    According to recent reports, FAA employees typically conduct risk assessments and coordinate with contractors, such as L3Harris technicians, on system maintenance or upgrades, according to The Professional Aviation Safety Specialists (PASS) union that represents FAA technicians. But in a statement, the union said that none of its FAA technicians were involved in the upgrades that led to the ground stop.

    According to recent reports, similarly, CNN reported that the router replacement at the remote radio communications site in El Dorado was done by an L3Harris engineer without direct FAA oversight. The union and two sources told CNN that the FAA technician merely escorted the contractor into the facility and then turned his attention elsewhere without knowing what work the contractor was doing.

    Industry observers note that to get a former insider perspective, Ars conducted a lengthy interview with Philip Mann, a principal consultant at Vector Strategic Consulting LLC, where he advises on aviation safety and AI governance. Mann previously worked at the FAA in multiple roles for 17 years, starting as a technician at Denver International Airport and eventually becoming a training program manager at the FAA Academy in Oklahoma City.

    (This interview has been condensed and edited for clarity.).

    Ars Technica: What do you see as some of the potential contributing factors that led to the nationwide ground stop?

    Philip Mann: I spent a lot of time as a technician, and then did a bunch of things in between. And later on, I was an instructor at the FAA Academy, and then I did training program management. So I’ve seen a lot of this from all sides about how it’s supposed to work, and the thing that stood out to me the most immediately when I saw this is the time during the day in which the work was being done.

    As an FAA technician, this is managed at the field person level. This is not like a top-down command-control thing. It is your job to cultivate a little credulity and think, “Okay, this thing I’m working on, what’s the worst thing that could happen? How far can it reach? What’s the blast radius?” This impacted a nationwide network, so by default the blast radius is the largest possible blast radius, so that basically means you take the maximum possible mitigations.

    Industry observers note that to kind of contrast that, when I worked at Denver [International Airport], a lot of times I was working on things that were on a single runway, like one approach lighting system or one electronic system, and the blast radius was just that runway, not even the whole airport, just that specific runway, and sometimes only that one end of that one runway. So you can still use the rest of it just fine.

    It has been revealed that and then maybe we work on a radar site, and a radar site might have a little more of a regional area. Most of the ones I worked on were kind of short-range radar, so it might be like a 50-mile radius or something. In which case you look at what the edges are, and you assume that if something goes wrong, that whole area just goes dark for air traffic controllers.

    So you plan around that, and the coordination goes on up to regional, national stuff like this. And this is the far end of that, just basic risk management stuff. The bigger the potential impact, the more people and operations potentially affected, the more you emphasize doing things like working at night when there’s less traffic, which is when this should have been done.

    And even Duffy has kind of acknowledged that [the FAA] confused the physical location of the facility with how far that system and service could reach within the national airspace system, and they had it completely backward. Yeah, on a map this is out in the middle of nowhere, but in a network diagram this router was immediately adjacent to all 22 of the [FAA’s air route traffic control] centers. Of those, 17 were affected, but it was immediately adjacent to all 22 of them.

    That was the thing that immediately struck me: How clear it is that basic impact analysis and basic risk management seems to have just been completely gone.

    Sources indicate that it even goes a little bit further than that. As a technician, we used to have this rule that you don’t break anything on a Friday. We would actually not schedule certain work past lunch, and it wasn’t to get people off early. It was basically because, if something broke, somebody was going to have to come in on Saturday to fix it. You break it Thursday, people are going to be in on Friday anyway.

    And then we had the commandment: “Thou shalt not be on the front page of the newspaper,” and it seems like all of that was missing here.

    L3Harris should know better, because Harris has a history. Back in 2009, they misconfigured something and caused a massive network outage. At the time, they had only identified a small handful—I want to say it was like a couple dozen potential areas of impact—and it wound up being like six times that. So they should know better.

    It has been revealed that (Ars note: The 2009 network incident was caused by a Harris technician incorrectly configuring a router that directs air traffic data through the FAA telecommunications network. That error ended up delaying thousands of travelers and grounded hundreds of flights nationwide.).

    I don’t know how it was done on site, but when I did this work, quite often when contractors were working, I was the person who was there that got them cleared to the fence, that got their badges, that got them scheduled, that did the coordination with the airport authorities, and whatever else we had to do.

    So there was always an FAA person that was the point of contact, and even on some facilities it might have to be an FAA person that physically pushes the button to turn the system back on. Like in a lot of cases, a contractor cannot do that, and it might be quite literally as simple as just flipping a switch. But the thing is, that action puts that system onto the national airspace system. That has to be done by the government. It can’t be done by a contractor.

    Now, I don’t know if that’s the case here. I’m just saying it’s typical.

    Ars Technica: The Professional Aviation Safety Specialists (PASS) union representing FAA technicians put out a statement saying that, “historically contractors have followed a protocol where FAA employees conduct a risk assessment and coordinate the maintenance of the system or equipment.” The union then noted that “PASS-represented technicians” were not involved in the upgrades on the “contractor owned and maintained routers” that led to the ground stop.

    Mann: In my experience, the union a lot of times is one of the groups that raises their hand and says, “Hey, hold on, we need a qualified person. What does that actually mean? Like, who on this list of people is qualified? Does that mean that they’ve had the class? Does that mean they’ve got a certification? Does that mean they’ve been here for a certain period of time?” But they’ll figure that out, and the answer is not always the same.

    So, in a different FAA system at a different time, we had to get somebody who had been to a specific set of schools and, in one case, some specific vendor schools. The FAA at that time had only sent like a half-dozen people through those schools because they’re really expensive and really long. They had a couple in the east, a couple in the west, a couple in the middle, and every time they did one of these projects they would grab one of those people and put them on there, because that’s what a qualified person is.

    Maybe they had somebody for the FAA that was there, but maybe that person was a newly introduced hire who was administratively qualified to be on site, meaning they had their background check and their driver’s license and had their access badges and all that. But maybe they didn’t even have a networking background or whatever. They were just the person who had the access and the free time and could be there.

    According to recent reports, but this is certainly a case, especially with the national-size blast radius of a network, that highlights the importance of having that qualified person, whatever that means. That is very much a union push to make sure that we know what the right qualified person means, that we know how to identify those people and that we’re treating those people fairly.

    According to recent reports, it’s vital to understand that in the union leadership, they’re all former technicians and engineers, everybody who runs that union. Even the local shop people are all fully qualified. So they all know what’s going on. Their role in all this potentially is to cover that blind spot that management and contractors share.

    Ars Technica: Based on what you described, it does sound like both the contractor side and the current FAA side were underestimating the potential blast radius for whatever reason.

    Sources indicate that mann: Well, yeah, and Duffy has even indicated that they mistook the physically remote location for being a network remote location, and those two don’t correspond to each other. Duffy has mentioned that it was the physical smallness and the physical remoteness of the site that somehow let them forget about what they were actually working on.

    Sources indicate that ars Technica: That’s kind of astounding, isn’t it? It’s like the current FAA leadership acknowledging that somehow they didn’t know about their own network and the importance of different nodes in the network.

    Mann: In recent years they’ve brought a lot more people into the fold with the FAA, and you can see that overall a lot of it is more Silicon Valley-type people. It’s not aviation people or risk people or even necessarily physical engineering people. And I make that separate distinction because physical engineering is way more rigorous than anything like software engineering—that’s hopefully public knowledge.

    But they get a lot of people who’ve got the “move fast, break things” approach that even [Mark] Zuckerberg stopped believing in. They’ve got the “deploy it now, patch it later” mindset, like “Oh well, we just reboot it, or if it goes down, we’ll just be down for a little while; we’ll lose a few ad dollars or whatever.”.

    But the national airspace system is a whole different animal, because the national airspace system has to work all the time.

    Industry observers note that it is possible to bring things down and to do it in a scheduled way. We would shut down radar sites on purpose, but we would also put NOTAMs [Notice to Airmen advisories] out saying, “Hey, this airspace is not covered by radar right now,” and some of that stuff is done weeks and weeks and weeks in advance.

    Now, at a national network scale, there’s not really a way to say, “By the way, just in case we might shut the NAS off, we might shut down all the airspace because we’re not sure if this one little router out in Arkansas someplace is going to cause problems.”.

    I have ideas about how this might have happened, but the long and short of it is, when they plugged it in, they didn’t adequately test it before they connected it back to the network some way somehow, and it could have been misconfigured. Maybe there was an approved configuration, somebody didn’t have it, so they just kind of winged it, or it could be that somebody got the wrong configuration. But again, we’ll wait for the root cause to come out, if it comes out sometime later.

    Ars Technica: What are the main things that should have been done to prevent this from becoming a whole nationwide incident?

    Mann: An notable caveat is, I don’t know if this was a misconfiguration or just somebody making a mistake, or just a bad configuration that shouldn’t have worked. I don’t know how much testing was done.

    But what should have happened is, with whatever necessary level of technician and engineer engagement, they should have done the blast radius assessment, the risk assessment. Duffy has already conceded they did not do a sufficient risk assessment. He has not stated it exactly that way, but he has said that they misunderstood the risk in not so many words. They should have pulled up the network topology and looked at what does this actually touch.

    One of the systems I used to work on a lot was backup power, so backup generators attached to a radar site. I was working on the generator, but I still marked the radar site as potentially out of service, because the power generator affects the radar site, and if the generator crashes, it’s going to take the radar site down.

    Sources indicate that so in a network, that’s just a million times more complex, because you really need to go, “How far could this reach?” You, of course, want to understand that at the networking level. You want to understand what all that is, but what they need to do is the proper risk assessment.

    Do whatever engineering, whatever tests, whatever scenario things they want to do and really, really, really embrace that it’s not what you’ve seen before. What is the boundary of what is prohibited by physics? You’re talking about an interconnected network. There is nothing in physics that claims a data bit from this router can’t get to the far end of the universe if they’re all connected. And thinking about that kind of stuff, assume it might fail.

    Recent findings suggest that that’s the first significant thing, and that should have taken whatever amount of time it took. Because the benefit with this kind of a system is that same basic impact assessment, you know, plus or minus maybe a couple of relatively small variables, is going to apply to every single one of these installations across the entire country. If they’re doing one of them or doing 1,000 of them, they’re all network-interconnected devices that all do the same thing and all hit the same network.

    In a recent development, so it sounds bad when you think about doing it for every single site separately, but when you do a full network analysis, you’re like, “We’ve got to do this really hard thing one time, and then we’ve got to assess to see if there’s been any changes as we migrate this network piece by piece.” Does the latest router significantly change anything? But it’s pretty easy from there.

    In a recent development, then, and this is the crucial part, then they need to behave as if they’re trying to keep that worst-case scenario thing from happening. Or even if they can’t keep it from happening, reduce the impact as much as possible.

    So do it at midnight when, if you have a complete mass outage like this, it’s not too many travelers. Maybe a couple red-eye flights, a few cargo planes like UPS, FedEx, because those guys fly at night a lot, but it’s not 12,000 passenger planes.

    In a recent development, that may not have prevented the absolute failure whenever we find out what that is, but it would have reduced how bad it got. If you’ve already done that kind of risk assessment, and you’ve briefed everybody accordingly, your technicians are sitting there in the building—hopefully they’re the right people—and they’re already braced to recover.

    In a recent development, every time I started an engine generator that was going to run a radar site, I would hold my breath for a second when I flipped a switch, because things can happen. You can do everything right, and you flip a switch, and the engine throws a rod or something. Nothing you could do about it. Nothing you would know to prevent or anything like that. But we would hold our breath for a second, make sure everything was operating fine. Go outside, look up, make sure the antenna is still spinning, all that kind of stuff.

    According to recent reports, it is the same kind of thing. These technicians, if they’re braced and ready to intercept the early signs of that worst case scenario failure, they’re not casual about it. They’re really thinking, “Okay, we need to watch this and look for any unusual behavior early, and then be ready to shut it back off or pull the plug or whatever if we start seeing something we’re not comfortable with.”.

    Industry observers note that you’re kind of chopping off the impact from both sides a little bit. Technicians are more prepared to catch it faster, and even if it goes for a little bit, it’s not going to affect nearly as many people.

    In a recent development, in this case it’s possible—don’t know but it’s possible—if this would have been at 2 or 3 o’clock in the morning, it might have started lighting up some lights somewhere, but they could have potentially shut it down, because you don’t have so many flights and data overloading the network. It’s possible, and just my speculation, it’s possible they could have seen it, flipped it off, let everything calm down, and not had a ground stop at all.

    Sources indicate that ars Technica: The router installation concern that led to the nationwide ground stop was part of an ongoing FAA effort to modernize its overall system. What might this event indicate about the current state of the US National Airspace System?

    Mann: This is one of the challenges with the FAA modernization. When they do that properly, nobody sees that there’s that kind of danger out there. It’s kind of the paradox of risk analysis, right? The better you are at it, the less essential people think it is, and that’s the FAA being a victim of its own success for the last 50 years. I’m not in that camp that everything that sounds old needs to be replaced. Floppy disks are totally fine as long as they still work, I don’t care.

    But the agency has had a hard time modernizing, in part, I believe, because it is so safe and its risk management is normally so good that people lose sight of the fact that there isn’t modernization that needs to be done.

The FAA is so good at what it does that when it comes time to write checks, there’s always a different squeaky wheel that needs the money more.

    Actually, I’m kind of happy for the current administration keeping this at the front. I don’t necessarily like how they’re doing it, but I do like that they’re making this a live issue in Congress. They’re making this a live issue even out here in different airports. I’ll talk to people and they’re like, “Hey, when are we going to modernize this?” Ten years ago, not too many people out in the public were talking about it.

    I think the NAS is still just as safe as it’s always been. We can kind of be grateful. Folks probably ought to understand that because they see this on the news, it means it’s weird. It’s unusual. But it’s good that we can be safe and we can still have the conversation about it, about what needs to happen to keep it safe, because we don’t want to have a catastrophic failure somewhere down the line that really is because something failed or really is because something was neglected, and then try to say, “Oh yeah, now we’ve got to shut down our airspace for six months because something happened.”.

    It has been revealed that I’m not a blank check person. I do not want [Congress] just writing a check and handing it to Duffy or anybody. I want them to do the proper acquisition oversight, do the proper union involvement, do the proper technical evaluations, all that kind of stuff, because that is money well spent.

    According to recent reports, we could have been really unlucky. We could have lost communication to all the aircraft that were in the air entirely. We could have lost the ability to be able to manage those aircraft, and then we would have been back to doing 1950s, 1960s kind of stuff, like call the airplane and have the airplane tell us where it is. And we probably would have seen some bad outcomes from that.

    Ars Technica: It is definitely sobering to think that this was in some ways the best-case scenario from the situation that unfolded.

    Mann: This was a best and worst [case]. In the resilience of the system, this was a best case because the system degraded all the way down to its essential mission of just keeping the aircraft safe. And an aircraft parked on the ground is as safe as it’s ever going to be, and the system was successful. The system is very resilient. In other words, it’s not intended to be used right now, but they’re putting in a placeholder.

    Sources indicate that if you’ve got a deployment, you’ve got three steps. You’ve got an A, B, C step. Well, if you need some ridiculously high-powered, super fast switch or something at step C, you might put that in at step A, knowing you’re not using its full capability, because that’s when it makes sense to do that. Maybe it’s difficult infrastructure, physically hard to do or whatever.

    Sources indicate that but you put the super-fast switch in it at A, then you do step B, then you do step C, and only at that time when you get to step C are you actually going to start using the capabilities in that switch. And those might be years apart. I can imagine something like that being a subtext.

    Industry observers note that but the thing is, the SMART system looks out weeks and months in the future. It doesn’t touch the operation. It reads data, it does some stuff and makes some advising comments and makes some advising predictions, and then tells the air traffic control center folks, “Hey, y’all might want to do this.”.

    To the best of my knowledge and in my opinion, the SMART system doesn’t touch the actual operational data. In other words, it’s not something that reaches out across the whole network. It has certain data sets that are at the control center or wherever it is. There’s certain data that it has access to that it cannot push information into. It just draws from data and does analysis, and then it provides a recommendation to the traffic managers, and then those traffic managers act or don’t act on that information in some way.

    SMART is a system that reads. You can think of it as a Wall Street guy who reads the ticker and makes some calculations and then hands a spreadsheet to the trader. The analyst is not the trader. The analyst is literally reading the screen, running some math, and then handing a ticket to the trader, and a trader makes the final decision.

    That’s kind of what happens where the system looks at what’s going on in NAS, what’s forecast to go on in NAS, weather, all that kind of stuff, and then it does some calculations and it effectively hands a slip of paper to the air traffic controllers and states, “Hey, you might want to do this.” But none of that would mean that it’s Skynet getting onto the network or something like that.

    In a recent development, this story was updated on November 20, 2026 to correct the description of the FAA ground stop’s impact on aircraft arrivals and departures. It was also updated to clarify one of Mann’s comments on the “move fast, break things” approach.

    #70275. How long can fiber optic cables be before they lose signal?

    📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (747 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Engadget ↗ Open Full Page

    How long can fiber optic cables be before they lose signal?

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (747 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Fiber optic cables are responsible for a significant portion of the world's Internet infrastructure.
    • According to recent reports, the longest fiber optic cable run in the world is the 2Africa cable system.
    • Industry observers note that as with any technology, fiber-optic cables have their limits.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Fiber optic cables are responsible for a significant portion of the world's Internet infrastructure. You may know that the technology is responsible for carrying data signals across oceans, but fiber has also become increasingly common in our cities and even homes. Many internet service providers (ISPs) use fiber-optic as a selling point, and for good reason: It offers a significant internet speed upgrade over legacy DSL connections that rely on copper telephone lines.

    According to recent reports, the longest fiber optic cable run in the world is the 2Africa cable system. It's an underwater optical fiber cable that has landing points in many African countries as well as Europe and Asia. The previous record was held by SEA-ME-WE 3, a cable system that connected portions of Europe, Northern Africa, the Middle East, Asia, and Australia. That system was decommissioned in 2024.

    Industry observers note that as with any technology, fiber-optic cables have their limits. So how long can a fiber-optic cable actually be before signal loss makes the data being transmitted completely unrecoverable?

    It has been revealed that fiber-optic cables rely on a physics principle called total internal reflection to transmit data through glass (or sometimes plastic) strands in the form of light. The glass core has a high enough refractive index so that when light hits the boundary at a sufficiently shallow angle, it reflects back into the core rather than passing through. This allows the light to travel long distances without experiencing significant energy loss or signal deterioration.

    Recent findings suggest that this is in stark contrast to Ethernet cables, which rely on twisted pairs of copper wires to transmit data in the form of electrical current. Like any metallic conductor, copper wires have some resistance, which means you can't use them for very long distances. The maximum recommended length for Cat5e Ethernet cables is just 100 meters or slightly over 300 feet. They're also affected by electromagnetic interference, affecting their reliability over long runs.

    Industry observers note that by comparison, fiber optic cables can carry data over several kilometers before the signal starts breaking down. A single fiber-optic cable can bundle multiple individual fibers, each capable of carrying its own data signals. This is why internet service providers advertise their use of fiber over traditional copper wiring when deploying city-wide networks. The end result is a much faster connection that's often more consistent.

    It has been revealed that however, fiber optic cables have limits too. Even with total internal reflection, a small amount of light is lost as it travels through the glass core due to absorption and scattering. This gradual reduction in signal strength is called attenuation. Over a long enough run, this weakens the signal until the receiver can no longer distinguish between useful data and noise.

    A single uninterrupted glass fiber can typically span several kilometers before signal loss becomes a limiting factor. Keep in mind, fiber-optic cables also come in two types: single-mode and multi-mode.

    According to recent reports, single-mode fiber only allows one beam of light to travel through it at a time, while multi-mode fiber allows multiple light pulses (called modes) to propagate through the strands simultaneously. These pulses take slightly different paths within the strand, which means they can arrive at different times. This is called modal dispersion and eventually causes the receiver to struggle interpreting the data signal.

    Single-mode fiber is capable of carrying signals over longer distances but requires specific equipment that can cost significantly more money. Multi-mode fiber cables have wider cores that makes optical alignment with transceiver equipment easier, so they're often the preferred choice for shorter fiber runs. With longer runs, though, single-mode fiber's stability can justify the higher equipment costs.

    Regardless of the operating mode, you likely won't have to worry about signal loss in a typical home network. Even multi-mode fiber can cover hundreds of meters. The bigger problem in a domestic fiber cable run is often caused by bends that are too tight, which can cause light leakage from the core.

    It has been revealed that in the case of fiber optic systems running across continents, they use optical amplifiers to compensate for signal loss over long distances. These devices are installed along the seabed and designed to boost the optical signal. A technique known as multiplexing then allows multiple data streams to travel simultaneously over a single strand. Put simply: You never have a truly uninterrupted fiber optic cable running over such vast distances.

    In a recent development, nikhil Gupta (seen in a 2024 courtroom sketch) pleaded guilty in a plot to kill Gurpatwant Singh Pannun, a U.S. resident who advocated for a sovereign Sikh state in northern India.

    Prosecutors alleged that in May 2023, Gupta was recruited by Vikash Yadav, an Indian intelligence officer, to carry out an assassination of Pannun.

    Yadav allegedly provided Gupta with personal information about Pannun, including his address in Latest York and information about his daily activities, prosecutors said.

    It has been revealed that at his handler's direction, Gupta contacted someone to facilitate the assassination, but that person was actually a US government informant, prosecutors mentioned. The informant introduced Gupta to a "hitman", who was actually an undercover officer with the Drug Enforcement Agency.

    Gupta was arrested in June 2023 at an airport in Prague, Czech Republic and extradited to the US. He has been held at a jail in Fresh York pending his sentencing Friday at a Manhattan court.

    "He thought that from outside this country he could kill someone in it without consequence, simply for exercising their American right to free speech," then-US attorney Jay Clayton remarked in a statement, after announcing Gupta's guilty plea.

    Following Gupta's arrest, a spokesperson for India's Ministry of External Affairs stated that Yadav is no longer employed, external by the Indian government.

    The country also set up an inquiry committee to address security concerns raised by the US, the spokesperson noted.

    Narinder Singh Randhawa, a Sikh separatist and successor of Hardeep Singh Nijjar as temple leader in Surrey, British Columbia, told the BBC the sentencing marks the "first time we see justice" against what he calls historic and systemic persecution of Sikhs by the Indian government in India and abroad.

    Inderjeet Gosal, another Sikh separatist advocate based in Ontario, called the sentencing "a big community event".

    "It's for all the community to finally witness someone getting caught red-handed.".

    Anthropic researcher uses AI to solve math's greatest riddle

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • A mathematician working for AI giant Anthropic claims he used the tech giant's Claude AI tool to solve one of mathematics most famous problems.
    • The Riemann hypothesis dates back to 1859 and centers on the distribution of prime numbers underpinning a much wider scope of mathematical work.
    • Levent Alpoge, a member of Anthropic's technical staff, made the announcement on his website.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A mathematician working for AI giant Anthropic claims he used the tech giant's Claude AI tool to solve one of mathematics most famous problems.

    The Riemann hypothesis dates back to 1859 and centers on the distribution of prime numbers underpinning a much wider scope of mathematical work.

    Levent Alpoge, a member of Anthropic's technical staff, made the announcement on his website. "I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis," Levent Alpoge wrote in a note released Friday.

    In a recent development, the proof still has to be verified and confirmed by other mathematicians. If it withstands independent examination, it would be a major milestone both in mathematics and the growing role of artificial intelligence (AI) in scientific research.

    The Riemann hypothesis is the latest and most vital in a string of famous mathematical problems that were tackled with the help of AI.

    Alpoge mentioned that the collaboration with AI had generated more than 250,000 pages of mathematical material, adding that he had not yet mastered all the mathematics involved.

    Sources indicate that "Claude and I have had a great time together with such breadth in recent months, but this time Claude far outpaced me near the finish line," he wrote. "No, Claude flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line.".

    The Riemann Hypothesis is one of seven major mathematical problems, the so-called Millennium Prize Problems, selected by the Clay Mathematics Institute, which offers $1 million for a solution to each of those.

    "This is an announcement of historic significance," Martin Bridson, president of the institute, mentioned in a statement quoted by news agency AP.

    He added it "holds the promise of a dramatic transformation in the perception of what is possible in the struggle to extend the human understanding of mathematics.".

    "But the journey from today’s announcement to a place of real understanding will be long and difficult.".

    Formulated by German mathematician Bernhard Riemann in the 19th century, the hypothesis is about the distribution of prime numbers, which are numbers that can only be divided by themselves and the number 1.

    Recent findings suggest that the hypothesis describes a fundamental pattern of how these numbers are distributed as they become ever larger. Confirming that hypothesis is thought to have crucial implications for a wide range of further mathematical research.

    The potential breakthrough by Alpoge and Claude AI comes amid a growing number of examples where artificial intelligence systems are making significant contributions to advanced mathematical research.

    In September, rival AI company OpenAI noted its technology had helped solve a problem involving the Navier-Stokes equations.

    The equations, which describe the movement of fluids such as water and air, are another of the seven Millennium Prize Problems, but the claim that they've been solved also still needs independent verification.

    Sources indicate that agents capable of computer work have become one of the hottest commodities in the tech industry over the past year. Major labs like Anthropic and OpenAI have launched such services, while other major tech brands — like Meta, which recently launched its Muse agent line — have also moved into the space. It makes sense that Apple — which is trying to expand its AI offerings in the new John Ternus era — would want to follow suit.

    Bloomberg additionally notes that, at the same time that Apple is working on its own digital assistant, the firm is making it significantly harder for third-party agents to gain total control over its computers.

    In a recent development, the outlet notes that the version of its upcoming macOS 27.3 will deploy warnings discouraging consumers from granting full access to third-party agents. In October, Apple issued a notification to developers stating that the manufacturer planned to “introduce additional controls to ensure that users who genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access can only do so with very explicit user action.”.

    Bloomberg writes that while the iPhone maker “has eyed introducing the service as soon as the end of next year,” progress on its in-house agent “remains in the early stages.”.

    “We are continuing to build more Steam Machine units, but memory and storage costs continue to increase at unprecedented levels,” Valve wrote in a blog post on Thursday. “As a result we don’t yet know the number we are able to make, and at what price we’ll be able to offer them. The 2TB model in particular will be especially constrained.”.

    If Valve does have to raise the price of the Steam Machine, it will be in good organization. All three major console manufacturers instituted historically atypical price increases in 2025, with additional price hikes happening this year.

    For the Steam Machine, though, Valve may be more susceptible to supply-related price shocks than its larger competitors in the gaming hardware space. Valve “likely [doesn’t] have the same kind of priority as a Nintendo, Sony, or Microsoft when it comes to suppliers,” F-Squared analyst Michael Futter told us earlier this year. And while the bigger players can still negotiate somewhat with chip suppliers, Valve’s Steam Machine is “a niche product that cannot benefit in the same way when it comes to procurement,” Niko Partners analyst Daniel Ahmad said.

    According to recent reports, while Valve has not publicly discussed total Steam Machine sales, estimates based on public Steam Top Sellers charts suggest the manufacturer was selling 12,000 to 15,000 a week back in July. By contrast, the PS5 has averaged over 300,000 weekly unit sales worldwide in its roughly six years on the market.

    For now, at least, Valve notes it has fulfilled an expectation it set in July that “everyone in the reservation queue will have the option to purchase by the end of this year.” The company now says there is “no waitlist remaining” for the 512GB Steam Machine model and that “purchase invites” have been sent to the remaining randomized 2TB reservation holders (who placed orders back in April). The 512GB model was even briefly back in stock on the Steam Store yesterday, even as Valve continues to pare down the waitlist for 2TB stock.

    Valve notes it aims to release additional updates on Steam Machine availability in January.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that remote access to a Raspberry Pi is invaluable for home projects when you can't access your device directly.
    • In a recent development, raspberry Pi Connect is a program created by Raspberry Pi that lets you communicate with your Pi unit over the internet from outside your network.
    • Raspberry Pi Connect leverages WebRTC, a peer-to-peer connection between two web browsers that runs through a secure tunnel.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Avoid forwarding ports by using this handy tool.

    Industry observers note that remote access to a Raspberry Pi is invaluable for home projects when you can't access your device directly. In the past, logging into your Pi meant setting up a VNC service or SSH tunneling, both of which require port forwarding. It can be a hassle for beginners and a potential security risk for certain projects. Thankfully, there's a better way to access your Raspberry Pi remotely without wrangling ports.

    In a recent development, raspberry Pi Connect is a program created by Raspberry Pi that lets you communicate with your Pi unit over the internet from outside your network. It's convenient, doesn't require port forwarding and lets you access your Pi when you're outside your network. The best part is that Connect works automatically with your device if it's running Bookworm or later. Older devices have limited options with Connect, but as long as you're running Pi OS or its Lite variant, you can set it up as quickly as running a few commands in an SSH terminal.

    Raspberry Pi Connect leverages WebRTC, a peer-to-peer connection between two web browsers that runs through a secure tunnel. It doesn't require any third-party software on your Pi unit, and its secure nature lets it bypass strict firewalls and restricted NATs. Since it runs over the internet, you will need internet access and a Raspberry Pi Connect account to use it.

    Sources indicate that connect offers two key features: screen sharing and remote shell. The remote shell acts as an SSH terminal that runs in your browser, making it ideal for monitoring or running commands remotely. Screen share lets you turn your browser into a remote desktop for your Pi. Screen shares run through a Wayland session, which will use the Pi's resources and require an active desktop session; remote shell does not. If you're using an older Pi model, be sure to upgrade its Pi OS if you want to use Connect's screen sharing feature. Pi OS Lite and X11 are not compatible with this feature.

    Using Raspberry Pi Connect is fairly easy. You'll need two things: Pi Connect installed on your Pi unit and an internet connection. Pi Connect comes in full and lite packages. The full package includes screen-sharing compatibility for Pi units connected to a display, while the lite package is for remote access only. To install the package, start an SSH session with your Pi unit and run the following:.

    After installing either package, type "rpi-connect on" to enable access to the internet.

    Industry observers note that now that Connect is ready, it's time to access your Raspberry Pi. Head to connect.raspberrypi.com and sign in to your Pi account. If you don't have one, you can create one from that menu. Once logged in, you'll need to link your Pi unit to your account. Specific instructions on how to link your Pi unit can be found on the Raspberry Pi website, located under the "Get Started" section. Once linked, sign in to your account, select the "Connect via" button, and then pick your preferred connection option. If you need to make further changes to your Raspberry Pi, you can do so easily by logging in and connecting to your device.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Trump claims he won't allow American companies to build data centres "outside" the US.

    Donald Trump has mentioned he will ban US companies from building AI data centres overseas, threatening a "tremendous tax" for tech firms who do so.

    "We're going to keep it all in this country," the US president mentioned, while providing little detail on the potential policy he said others in his cabinet were hearing about for the first time.

    Data centres were a central issue in the midterm elections earlier in November, with many Democratic candidates promising tougher regulation on their construction.

    Tech giants including Meta and Google have entered agreements to build data centres overseas. It remains unclear how such a policy would be enforced if it was brought in.

    "We're not going to allow our companies to build data centres outside of our country," Trump told reporters in a press briefing following his return from his trip to Asia.

    "Because China will take all of them, and we're not allowing that to happen.".

    But whether that idea will become policy remains unclear.

    "I don't know if that's a breaking story, but I haven't even mentioned that to my people. But I'm telling them now, they're here," he said.

    Trump floated the policy after saying the US was leading on data centre construction, and he would not allow China to beat the US when it came to AI - which he calls super intelligence, or SI.

    It also follows an announcement earlier this week that would restrict the export of advanced computer chips and who can access the computing power provided by them.

    Washington on Monday unveiled firms would require a licence to buy advanced chips, so US officials can monitor whether they are being used to serve Chinese companies or they are being smuggled into China.

    The move will impact South East Asian countries that have invested heavily in data centres, as Chinese companies seek to rent computing power from overseas.

    Why Canada is embracing AI data centres while the US pushes back.

    Data centres are crucial to the AI boom. The vast warehouse-style buildings house the advanced computer chips and servers that are needed to run AI programmes such as Claude and ChatGPT.

    As of April there were about 3,000 data centres across the US, with another 1,500 in various stages of approval and construction, according to the Pew Research Centre.

    Many of them are built in rural areas, and concerns about challenges including noise pollution and energy consumption helped drive Democratic candidates promising tougher rules on data centre construction to wins on 3 November.

    "You ought to take advantage of the data centres. Make them pay you, make them pay your community, but take advantage don't shut them off," Trump remarked.

    According to recent reports, "We have a lot of places that want them badly, and they're great places. They have energy and they have everything. They're tremendous assets.".

    Large tech firms - often called AI hyperscalers due to the size of their investments in AI - have also been branching out, and Canada has made moves to step in to offer itself as an alternative location for these sites, with less local pushback against projects so far.

    Meta has already broken ground on a data centre, external in the province of Alberta, and Anthropic has signed a long-term agreement to lease a proposed data centre in Nova Scotia.

    The BBC has reached out to Meta for comment on Trump's remarks.

    In September Google unveiled a â¬13bn ($15bn: Â£11bn) investment in AI infrastructure in Finland, which included funding for three data centres.

    Last month, building work for two of those centres was halted due to concerns over the clearance of more than 300 hectares of forest.

    Trump called out the build in Finland specifically, saying his administration was "not allowing that to happen".

    Google has been contacted for comment.

These two cyberattacks follow recent network outages with other major US agencies that caused serious disruptions across the country. The National Security Agency experienced an outage that left its internal network offline for several days earlier this week, while the Federal Aviation Administration issued a nationwide ground stop last week.

    White House national cyber director Sean Cairncross will be stepping down from his role, Axios reported. The news comes as Democrats prepare to take control of Congress and as businesses across the country report a flurry of technical outages whose cause remains unknown.

    According to recent reports, cairncross, the president’s principal adviser on national cybersecurity policy and strategy, took office in August 2025. Since then, he has met with top AI leaders and helped the Trump administration make key AI decisions, according to Axios. The outlet also reports that the split between Cairncross and the White House was amicable, and his departure was timed so that the White House could nab a Senate confirmation for his role before Democrats take control of Congress in January.

    Cairncross, a lawyer and longtime Republican operative, had no cybersecurity background when the Senate confirmed him 59–35. He previously served as the Republican National Committee’s chief operating officer and, during Trump’s first term, as CEO of the Millennium Challenge Corporation, a federal foreign aid agency. The office hasn’t been around long; Congress created it in early 2021, and Cairncross was only its third Senate-confirmed director. The first director, Chris Inglis, left after about 19 months, and the job then went about 10 months without a permanent director.

    We’ve reached out to the White House for comment.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • GiveSendGo has been accused of facilitating the financing of extremism, but the platform says it does not ‘condone racism, discrimination, hate speech, or violence of any kind’.
    • Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast.
    • Australian neo-Nazis have raised hundreds of thousands of dollars on the global crowdfunding platform GiveSendGo, which has been accused of facilitating the financing of hate and extremism.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    GiveSendGo has been accused of facilitating the financing of extremism, but the platform says it does not ‘condone racism, discrimination, hate speech, or violence of any kind’.

    Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast.

    Australian neo-Nazis have raised hundreds of thousands of dollars on the global crowdfunding platform GiveSendGo, which has been accused of facilitating the financing of hate and extremism.

    Of the 68 Australian fundraisers on the site, the White Australia party has raised the fourth-highest amount of money with $200,000 for its high court battle to overturn its ban as a designated hate group.

    Neo-Nazi Thomas Sewell’s legal defence fund is sixth at almost $110,000. Sewell pleaded guilty to violent disorder in October. He and others allegedly stormed Camp Sovereignty in 2025 after taking part in an anti-immigration march. Five people were injured.

    Recent findings suggest that giveSendGo was set up after GoFundMe started cracking down on hate groups. It notes its aims are to “share the Hope of Jesus through crowdfunding” and to “stand for freedom”.

    Most crowdfunding on the site is for uncontroversial causes – medical procedures, funerals for relatives, saving endangered species or creative projects.

    Other asks are overtly political – the top Australian fundraisers are from anti-trans and anti-abortion activists.

    Last year a Minnesota woman who admitted calling a child the N-word raised more than US$750,000 on the site to “protect [her] family”.

    The co-founder of GiveSendGo, Jacob Wells, defended hosting that fundraiser, saying he believed in “freedom of speech, freedom of association” and that those were foundational tenets of society.

    In a recent development, in 2022 the US Anti-Defamation League (ADL) Centre on Extremism found GiveSendGo hosted 230 campaigns “operated by or for extremists and their causes”. The centre found crowdfunding platforms had raised more than US$6m for extremist campaigns, and GiveSendGo was responsible for collecting more than 86.5% of that money from 2016 to 2022.

    “Extremist campaigns found on these platforms espouse hateful rhetoric including antisemitism, white supremacy, QAnon conspiracies and anti-LGBTQ+ extremism, as well as rhetoric from antisemitic sects of Black Hebrew Israelites,” it found.

    In 2023, the Australia/Israel & Jewish Affairs Council (Aijac) called on the Conservative Political Action Conference (CPAC) Australia – which that year featured the Coalition senator Jacinta Nampijinpa Price and former prime minister Tony Abbott – to dump GiveSendGo as its gold sponsor because of its use by neo-Nazis and other extremist groups.

    A spokesperson for GiveSendGo stated it did not “condone racism, discrimination, hate speech, or violence of any kind”.

    In a recent development, “We also do not allow fundraisers that promote or glorify violence, raise money for illegal activity, or mislead givers. We follow the laws of the countries we operate in, and we review every reported fundraiser against our terms of service,” the spokesperson remarked.

    “Fundraisers that violate those rules are subject to moderation or removal.”.

    Dr Matt Wade, a senior lecturer in social inquiry at LaTrobe University, has studied the interaction between crowdfunding platforms and extremist movements.

    Speaking broadly about GiveSendGo, not specifically about Australia, he said platform’s policies and how they are enforced had “gravely serious implications” and that GiveSendGo’s claim to be a free speech defender made it a “safe haven for white supremacist and neo-Nazi causes”.

    Hosting a fundraising campaign tacitly lent any cause legitimacy, he said.

    “Crucially, in key cases that are harbingers of growing far-right influence, these donations are not simply expressions of sympathy or support, but outright endorsements of the actions that the beneficiaries took,” he mentioned.

    GiveSendGo claims in its terms of service that it reviews every fundraiser and verifies the recipient’s identity, and that funds are disbursed to the recipient only once they have completed a compliance process.

    It expects donors to give only to those they know and trust, and does not confirm that every statement in a fundraiser is true.

    It bans any fundraisers for abortion, gender reassignment for minors and anything illegal.

    The spokesperson noted people had a right to ask for help, others had the right to decide whether to give, and that GiveSendGo was “not a place of judgment but a place of generosity”.

    Wade said GiveSendGo’s claim to ban the promotion of racism was questionable.

    “Many would argue that, at best, the qualifier of ‘stated or demonstrable purpose’ is wilfully naive and far too narrowly construed, given the ultimate aspirations and raison d’être of some of the figures they host on their platform,” he said.

    The top Australian fundraiser at the moment on the site is for Sall Grover, founder of the Giggle for Girls app, with almost $2m raised. Grover is fighting the federal court finding that her app discriminated against trans woman Roxanne Tickle.

    Next is the anti-abortion activist Joanna Howe, who has raised almost $400,000 to pursue legal action under the Fair Work Act against her employer, Adelaide University, because of its investigations into almost 200 allegations against her.

    Her husband, James Howe, has raised another $180,000 for a potential defamation case.

    Both Howes say on the site they would use any money left over to “transition” their careers.

    It has been revealed that the Sedra family has raised about $340,000 for help to “move to a safe home”. Andrew and Noleen Sedra, a married couple who are both pastors at the Pentecostal Echo church in Sydney, claim they were threatened at their home by “LGBTQ left-wing activists”. Other reports have cast doubt on that claim.

    The Sedras were contacted for comment.

    In a swirl of questions, fears, and outrage, the US Army unveiled Thursday that it would delay a plan to blow up 68 deteriorating barrels of lead azide, which would launch toxic gas and lead into the air. A federal appeals court further halted plans later on Thursday with an emergency order. The plume, containing neurotoxic lead, could potentially drift 100 miles north of the Army installation housing it in Middletown, Iowa, according to modeling released by the Army earlier this week.

    In a recent development, the Army had planned to carry out two controlled detonations, set off simultaneously around noon Friday, to destroy the barrels where they lie, which is in earth-covered concrete containment structures (called earth-covered magazines or ECMs). Prior to the court stay, the Army rescheduled the blast until November 23 to provide more time to communicate about the situation with Iowans, who have reported being unaware of the detonations until earlier this week.

    Sources indicate that “Public communication is essential to public trust,” Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle said in a post on social media at 7:31 pm ET Thursday. “Therefore, the Army will continue to actively engage with state and local officials throughout the region to distribute accurate, up-to-date information.”.

    Telle claimed that the Army could not delay the detonation any further than Monday due to the state of deterioration of the compound, which is extremely explosive and sensitive. “This will delay the detonation until the latest possible moment prior to a forecasted temperature drop, which would risk further destabilization of the material.”.

    Lead azide is a compound used in detonators for munitions and is stockpiled by the US military. In March, the US Army identified that the stockpile in the Iowa facility—the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant (IAAAP)—had deteriorated. The lead azide in the 68 barrels, reported to total around 9,700 pounds (4.4 tons), is suspended in a mixture of water and ethanol within the ECMs, but has degraded and crystallized over time. Temperature fluctuations can cause lead azide to dissolve into the water/alcohol solution and recrystallize into needles or platelets, the Army noted. In crystallized forms, lead azide becomes extremely sensitive to any physical shock, friction, or heat. The Army determined the current state is a “catastrophically hazardous condition.”.

    Industry observers note that in an environmental assessment released Wednesday, the Army mentioned that trying to move the lead azide from its current position for any reason was ruled out. Any sloshing or physical shock from loading, transporting, or burying the barrels for safer detonation would create “an unacceptable safety risk and a high probability of accidental, uncontrolled detonation.”.

    The military considered neutralizing the lead azide using a chemical reagent, but again ruled it out because it said the process would require handling the lead azide over an extended period, with barrels neutralized at a rate of 3 to 10 per day. “The chemical neutralization process requires significantly more ‘hands-on’ time and physical manipulation of the drums by personnel over a prolonged 7- to 22-day period, drastically increasing the probability of accidental, fatal detonation during handling,” the Army wrote in its assessment.

    In all, the Army considered a controlled, mitigated “Blow-in-Place” strategy the best option, and it specifically planned for a fall detonation. The Army stated the fall weather would “take advantage of periods of reduced thermal cycling and to ensure the lowest impact to facility operations and local agriculture (harvesting).”.

    According to an emergency permit for the detonation from the Environmental Protection Agency, the plan is to place explosive charges and an accelerant on or near each of the ECMs.

    The Army intends to try to mitigate the detonation’s impact with a few simple methods. Those include lime-fill and sand-fill barriers around the ECMs, water cannons and misters to control lead dust in the wake of the explosion, and timing the detonation with ideal weather conditions—avoiding high winds that could increase the area exposed to the plume or, conversely, a thermal inversion that could trap the plume in one place.

    Modeling released Wednesday—based on the conditions for the scheduled detonation on Friday—suggested the plume could deposit lead dust at an amount between 5 and 100 micrograms per square foot in a stretch up to 25 miles north, nearly to Wapello, Iowa. Those levels are above those considered hazardous for floors and windows, respectively. Meanwhile, airborne lead, at a level of 0.18 micrograms per cubic meter, would reach nearly 100 miles north, toward Cedar Rapids, Iowa. The EPA standard for lead levels in the air is 0.15 micrograms per cubic meter.

    During the detonation, the Army advised residents in the immediate area to consider leaving or at least staying indoors with windows closed. It also recommended people wash their cars if they park outside. Similarly, local fire departments reportedly planned to hose down children’s playgrounds to remove any coating of lead dust in the aftermath, and schools planned closures.

    The Army’s proposal was to communicate clearly with the public about the aims, including holding an open-house event on October 15. But while Middletown residents may have been aware of the detonations, Iowans in the projected path of the plume were surprised by the news this week.

    Recent findings suggest that in its environmental risk assessment, the Army said it planned to mitigate the lead fallout with “rapid excavation” of soil and dust and treat it with a “stabilization agent.” This was to prevent it from remaining in the environment of the military facility, from which it could drift or make its way into groundwater. But the efforts would not mitigate the airborne plume, and lead does not break down in the environment. Children and pregnant people are particularly vulnerable to the neurotoxic effects.

    Amid health and environmental fears, state leaders and residents raised a range of questions Wednesday and Thursday, from how the lead azide was allowed to deteriorate to its current hazardous condition and whether the Army had truly exhausted safer options—options that wouldn’t launch a toxic cloud over a swath of the state.

    Iowa’s governor-elect, Rob Sand, wrote on social media that an “unacceptable lack of communication and clarity has made Iowans understandably concerned and angry about this situation.”.

    Political leaders in nearby Illinois also chimed in, sending a letter to Telle and EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin, expressing “grave concerns” over the initiative.

    “Alongside our neighbors in Iowa, we are also demanding answers about how this could affect our people’s health and safety,” Illinois Governor JB Pritzker wrote on social media.

    According to recent reports, on Thursday, prior to the announcement of a delay, environmental groups filed a lawsuit seeking a court-ordered pause of the detonation. The groups alleged, in part, that the EPA approved the plan “without full consideration of less dangerous alternatives that would avoid widespread dispersal and deposition of toxic lead; and inadequate public notice of the plan to open-detonate hazardous waste due to the extraordinarily rushed timeline set by the Army.” Late Thursday, a federal appeals court issued an emergency stay of the Army’s EPA permit for the demolition, halting plans until it can review the case.

    Friday morning, the Army, Department of Health and Human Services, and EPA released a joint statement saying:.

    According to recent reports, the entire interagency is working together to ensure that the controlled detonation in Middletown, Iowa is conducted in the safest fashion possible. Officials have been meticulously planning for this event since March, and all agencies involved are prepared to take the most extreme mitigation measures available to ensure there is no risk to the public and any disruptions are minimized. The entire Trump administration will continue to engage with state and local officials, as well as the broader community, to keep all apprised of updates as they arise.

    Notably, in June, Zeldin listed the EPA’s work with Iowa’s lead azide as one of the top “100 environmental victories that showcase EPA’s unwavering dedication to protecting American families.” The work was number 60 on the list, described as providing “critical emergency support to Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, deploying technical experts for 68 deteriorating drums of explosive lead azide.”.

    This post was updated November 20 to include that the federal appeals court granted a stay in the case brought by the environmental groups.

    This built-in windows tool can tell if your DirectX has a problem

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (614 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
