    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The Anthropic IPO raises substantial questions about the future of AI, the firm’s safety-first mission, and how we balance idealism with capitalism.
    • Today, I’m talking with Hayden Field, The Verge’s senior AI reporter, about the Anthropic IPO for the third and final episode in our series about AI in real life.
    • The AI lab behind Claude went public on the Nasdaq last Thursday.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The Anthropic IPO raises substantial questions about the future of AI, the firm’s safety-first mission, and how we balance idealism with capitalism.

    Today, I’m talking with Hayden Field, The Verge’s senior AI reporter, about the Anthropic IPO for the third and final episode in our series about AI in real life.

    The AI lab behind Claude went public on the Nasdaq last Thursday. The numbers are gigantic, but not really that notable for this conversation, except to say that Anthropic has become one of the most valuable companies on the planet.

    It has been revealed that the real story is what happens now — and whether Anthropic can continue to thread the needle of caring about and investing in AI safety while also being a public tech giant beholden to shareholders. Oh, and it also continuously growing the amount of money it makes so it can keep paying its ever-increasing compute bills, which total roughly $900 billion over the coming years.

    All of these ideas sit in a fascinating tension with one another, and so Hayden and I really tried to break down how we think this might play out as Anthropic navigates the pressures of the public markets.

    You’ll hear us talk about the organization’s unique corporate governance structure, something that is especially relevant in the wake of the ongoing Jensen Huang saga. We also get into why OpenAI seems happy to have let Anthropic go public first, and why Anthropic’s whole pitch to big customers boils down to the same safety branding that now sits in conflict with the profit-oriented part of its business.

    Sources indicate that okay: Hayden Field, The Verge’s senior AI reporter, on the Anthropic IPO and the economics of frontier AI. Here we go.

    This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.

    Hayden Field, welcome back to Decoder.

    I’m excited to talk to you today because it’s not pure soap opera drama chaos.

    It’s like a normal thing that happened.

    It’s for once not personality-based and soap opera. It’s about cold, hard would-be cash.

    Industry observers note that [Laughs] Well, there is some personality in it because we’re going to talk a lot about Anthropic’s IPO, which has a bunch of big personalities in it, and the way they have structured this company to repel the rapacious pressures of capitalism is, I would say, very eccentric. It reflects the beliefs of a number of eccentric people.

    Yep, absolutely. It’s really been interesting digging into the S-1 again and just seeing who was on what committee and which founders have the most control here and how much control the founders actually have, which is more than it may seem.

    Sources indicate that let’s start at the start. You and I are talking on IPO day. Anthropic is the first pure AI lab to go public. They priced the IPO at $83 a share and they got all the way up to $111. By the time people are listening to this, who knows what the price will actually be, but it’s been a real victory lap for all the people who are invested in Anthropic. A bunch of law firms have changed their homepages to be like, “Congratulations, guys!”.

    Recent findings suggest that what do you make of this? Is it just the thing that had to happen or is it a sign that the AI bubble is not going to pop? How should people think about it?

    It has been revealed that I don’t think it really gives us latest information about whether the AI bubble is going to pop or not, because I mean, this is peak AI hype right here. It’s the first AI lab to go public. It’s been kind of on track to break records for months. Everyone was like, “It’s probably going to beat Musk,” and then it did. I can’t wait to see his tweets later.

    But the other interesting part of this is that I’ve heard thousands of upcoming millionaires and hundreds of new centimillionaires will be born from this, not to mention billionaires, too. It’s one of those things where I think the AI bubble is continuing to swell.

    I was even chatting with some tech workers inside a bunch of different companies this morning, and they were all saying within their companies, they’re seeing the bubble swell and swell, and they’re being tasked with doing more and more AI, even if it makes them less productive and makes the work less good.

    In a recent development, so I think there’s going to be a reckoning eventually, but right now we’re at peak AI hype and Anthropic does a great job of marketing its business as safe AI. Of course, they’re going to have more pressure around that marketing term now more than ever. So it’s going to be interesting to see the tension point kind of go into the spotlight and see how they handle this.

    Sources indicate that I was at the Semafor conference earlier this week. I saw Sam Altman and Sarah Friar, OpenAI’s CFO, on stage there. Altman and Greg Brockman were at the DealBook conference this week. I get the sense they’re kind of happy that Anthropic went first to see what happens in the markets and to see how companies value the revenue potential of their substantial competitors so they can tell their IPO story better.

    Is that the sense you get, that Anthropic is the trial balloon? Or is OpenAI just retconning the fact that it didn’t go first?

    Yes, I think that’s absolutely the case. I heard there was a time in the past year that Altman was really obsessed with beating Anthropic to go public. That’s what I heard. It was all he thought about. But then with all the bad press around OpenAI this year, they’ve had setback after setback. A lot of the public is particularly focused on hating OpenAI right now.

    Obviously, there’s a big AI populism backlash and a lot of people hate a lot of AI, but it seems like OpenAI has really borne the brunt of a lot of public hatred and scandals this year. And so they were like, “You know what? Let’s just take a step back and let Anthropic go first.” And they seem happy to do that.

    Industry observers note that now that Anthropic has gone first and set this historic precedent, OpenAI can ride on its coattails and say, “Yeah, us too.” I doubt they would beat Anthropic’s record. Maybe they will, maybe they won’t. But either way, I think they know that things could have gone a lot worse for them if Anthropic did not go first, if it’s happening this year.

    I can’t stop thinking about Anthropic in terms of just dumb business fundamentals now that it’s a public company. You buy a token from them. They have to make that token for less than you pay for it. They also want to make AGI. Somewhere else they have some other huge set of costs.

    Just based on what we know about the business today, now that it’s a public firm, are they profitable on the face of it? Do they have a long way to go before inference is so profitable it can pay for training all the latest models? How does their business actually work?

    Industry observers note that they have a long way to go and that is why it’s going to be so interesting to see what exactly they do here with regard to driving more revenue, which is what they’re going to have to do. I saw one estimate from Steve Rattner saying Anthropic is going to have to increase its revenue roughly 17-fold within the next 10 years to deliver a comparable return to some of its competitors in the tech industry.

    Industry observers note that but even without that specific number, you can tell. I mean, when a company goes public, investors want to see a return on their investment. They want to see profits go up or just profits at all. They also want to see that even if profits aren’t a thing yet, they want to see that you’re driving so much revenue that they could see profit happening in the near term. That is something that Anthropic is going to have to reckon with more than ever before after today.

    Industry observers note that I was chatting with a bunch of corporate governance experts and law professors and they were all saying Anthropic, like OpenAI, has such an unusual corporate structure that they aren’t actually beholden to shareholders in the way that some public companies are. Shareholders can never vote out executives. They don’t have a lot of power to influence anything really. It’s the founders and this special trust, which we can get to in a second, that have the power.

    Recent findings suggest that but either way, they were all saying it doesn’t matter if shareholders have a say here really in voting. It’s about the fact that no matter who has a say, Anthropic is going to be under so much pressure to make money and to buy compute and catch up with OpenAI in that way, that this is going to be a huge reckoning for them. We’re probably going to see a lot of things fall by the wayside, maybe even some expensive safety efforts.

    I want to come to the governance structure angle here. We live in a time of Nvidia scandals. Corporate governance is all the rage now. It’s the hottest topic in American business, but let’s come to that in one minute.

    I just want to stay on “can you sell a token for a dollar more than it cost you to make it” for one more turn. It’s just the dumbest way of thinking about this. Anthropic rents capacity from major cloud providers, from hyperscalers. They run the GPUs in them. They pay for power, they pay for the GPUs. There’s some input cost and then they have to sell the token for more than all those input costs.

    Recent findings suggest that that is the dumbest way of thinking about their business. I promise you that they think about it in a more sophisticated way than that, but that is how I think about it. I was just at the Microsoft Ignite conference this week and I saw Satya Nadella and he was very clear to me and others that they’re going to try to bring the price of tokens down, that their whole system is designed to make all the AI vendors fungible underneath Copilot and they’ll pick the best model for the task and make sure you get the cheapest one for whatever it is you’re trying to do.

    That seems totally at odds with what Anthropic needs to do, which is get more and more margin for every single token they sell so they can keep renting capacity from data centers or buy more chips than OpenAI or whatever it is they need to do. How are they structured to solve that problem? Is it just more people using AI or is it more expensive tokens?

    I think it’s a little of both, and it’s interesting because Anthropic has been kind of sneakily trying to do this. We wrote a piece in the past year about how there was a big outcry, particularly focused on Anthropic, for passing on costs to consumers. Individuals who were customers of Anthropic were really mad because they felt like the prices were going up for the same stuff or for worse quality and that costs were just getting passed on to them.

    It has been revealed that this became a thing across the industry, a significant outcry, but Anthropic bore the brunt of it. Anthropic had to have a public statement. They’re like, “Look, we’re going to work on this.” And they did roll it back a little, but I mean, they’ve got to keep doing it in some way.

    Industry observers note that the other thing they’re focused on is hoping that their models are going to be good enough that people just form an attachment — not emotionally, well maybe — but form an attachment to them and they can moat people in. They’re all about the moat these days: “We’ve got to build a moat.” OpenAI is about this, too. They want so much of your everyday life and business to be married to Anthropic’s tools that it’d be really hard to port it all over and you won’t want to and you’ll just keep paying. So that’s what they’re going for.

    Sources indicate that they’re also, of course, hoping that enterprise and government contracts are going to really make up a bunch of this, in which case you don’t have to worry quite as much about nickel-and-diming because they’ve got a lot of money. But I think that’s the interesting part here. When it comes to people that do care about the price a lot, they’re just trying to moat them in and hope for the best.

    What’s interesting there is that consumers are sensitive to price in one way. I think Anthropic’s major business customers, which is where they’ve been historically focused, are sensitive to price in different ways.

    Industry observers note that if you’re paying Anthropic a lot of money, you might want to be able to switch providers quickly and you might demand data sovereignty and all this stuff that significant enterprises are thinking about. Anthropic either has to deliver that, which would kill their moat for their big enterprise customers, or say, “We’re so good, you can’t have that.” I’m not sure that they can say the second one yet.

    That’s why they’re marketing this safe, trustworthy AI line so deeply, because it’s the only thing they’ve really got going for them here. When you have an enterprise customer, most of the time you do have to give them data sovereignty. You can’t trade on their data. There’s a lot of stuff that Anthropic could be doing to make more money that they can’t do when someone is paying that much.

    I think that’s really why they’re driving home this point of being the safe, trustworthy alternative because that’s the only thing that’s really going to get people to stick around, particularly if they also drive home the cybersecurity tools in an age when everything’s getting hacked all the time.

    The other interesting thing is even not with huge enterprises, but with small to medium-sized businesses, I’ve been chatting with a bunch of them and they’ve all been creating their own internal tools to kind of track which tasks they need specifically to use an expensive Anthropic model for and which ones they can port over to maybe an open-source model or a really cheap model.

    So a lot of companies like law firms — and people in a lot of different industries that have small to medium-sized businesses — are literally creating their own internal benchmarks about, “Okay, let’s save money as much as we can to just only put 10 percent of our tasks toward the expensive Anthropic model, and then this 40 percent can go to an open-source model and this 50 percent can go to a mid-tier, cheaper model.”.

    So that’s what’s really interesting to me. People are trying to figure this out on their own and not even sharing those benchmarks publicly because it’s their own way of budgeting.

    I actually heard Nadella this week say every manufacturer will have its own set of evaluations and they will test the models against them and always use the most efficient one and this will become one of the major things that every company does.

    The flip side to that is I’ve heard Anthropic executives say, “Well, you will always want the frontier model because your competitor will always be using the frontier model and if you use a cheaper one, you’ll be left behind.” And that has always seemed somewhere between naive and idealistic to me because I think a lot of companies do cheap things knowing that their competitors will also do cheap things.

    I agree completely. Everyone’s being cheap.

    Industry observers note that yeah, I think if you can get away with good enough, you’re going to find out exactly where good enough is and you will not assume that your competitor is going to eke out a 5 percent advantage by using a more expensive model. Somewhere on the margin is where all of the costs should be and the market will figure it out.

    It just feels like the basics of the business, maybe on IPO day, the pressure isn’t on that, everyone’s just very happy and rich. The next quarter’s earnings are going to be where we start to see this shakeout. Can it keep growing the way it’s growing at the margins it needs to build everything, especially when its own suppliers are now major shareholders?

    Totally. And we saw one quarter where they experienced huge growth and then the next quarter wasn’t that much. So yeah, I mean they’re going to have a lot to reckon with.

    Let’s talk about the governance complications. Because of Nvidia, corporate governance is the hottest topic in American business. Like you said, OpenAI and Anthropic have some of the most complicated governance structures in history.

    If you think that Anthropic’s future is to sell the best intelligence — the most capable, the most cutting-edge frontier, close-to-AGI intelligence possible — you would probably not do a bunch of safety work. You would probably not kill your margins on a bunch of researchers who are telling you to stop or slow down or not release the best model.

    It has been revealed that anthropic is deeply committed to doing that. You and I have had conversations before about whether that can withstand the pressures of capitalism and growth. That was hard when they weren’t a public organization, but now they are. Talk about Anthropic’s structure and how they’re trying to codify their commitment to safety.

    According to recent reports, yeah, that’s a really great question. I just published a piece about this. It’s so interesting to me that Anthropic, despite seeing all the roller-coaster drama that OpenAI went through around the Sam Altman ouster and all of the restructurings that that company has gone through, Anthropic has a similarly unusual structure. And in a way it’s helpful because they’re not beholden, as we said, to shareholder pressure besides if shareholders start selling off their stock or don’t buy more.

    But the two kinds of groups of people that have power over what happens at Anthropic are the founders and this group called the Long-Term Benefit Trust (LTBT). Anthropic likes to market this as being like, “Oh, don’t worry about that the founders are doing what’s best for humanity but with no checks. We’ve got this trust above us that can appoint or remove us anytime.” As we’ll see in the movie Artificial, Sam Altman famously claims, “Oh, well, the board can fire me whenever.” He says that a million times.

    Now, Anthropic is implying the same thing: “Oh, we have this trust above us. They can remove or appoint the majority of board members,” even though it’s actually not all of them, but we’ll get to that in a minute. So this trust is a group of right now four people and none of them have a lot of AI experience. It’s [former Federal Reserve Chairman] Ben Bernanke, a foreign policy analyst named Richard Fontaine, an experimental physicist named Christopher Stubbs, and a former GiveWell executive named Neil Buddy Shah, who is chair of the LTBT.

    I spoke to a couple of former Anthropic employees that left not too long ago and one of them mentioned that this trust is kind of handpicked to not rock the boat at Anthropic. The founders appointed them. They’re not going to be appointing someone that’s going to probably disagree with them a lot.

    According to recent reports, ironically, the trust doesn’t have the authority to step in on everyday decisions at Anthropic, unlike even the OpenAI nonprofit board that existed.     Startup sues Apple in India over tap-to-share contacts feature

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Apple is being sued in India by a U.S.-based startup that alleges the iPhone maker’s NameDrop feature, which lets customers share contact information by bringing devices close together, infringes its patented technology.
    • GG Technologies, the startup behind StayTouch, an app that lets people exchange contact details by bringing their phones close together, is seeking ₹15 billion (about $161.86 million) in damages and an injunction against Apple, per court documents reviewed by TechCrunch.
    • Santa Monica-headquartered GG Technologies filed the lawsuit in India in October after mediation proceedings initiated in April failed in September, the startup told TechCrunch.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Apple is being sued in India by a U.S.-based startup that alleges the iPhone maker’s NameDrop feature, which lets customers share contact information by bringing devices close together, infringes its patented technology.

    GG Technologies, the startup behind StayTouch, an app that lets people exchange contact details by bringing their phones close together, is seeking ₹15 billion (about $161.86 million) in damages and an injunction against Apple, per court documents reviewed by TechCrunch.

    Santa Monica-headquartered GG Technologies filed the lawsuit in India in October after mediation proceedings initiated in April failed in September, the startup told TechCrunch. Pre-institution mediation is generally required before filing commercial lawsuits in India. The company also sued Apple in the U.S. in April over related patent infringement claims.

    In its 781-page court filing in the Bombay High Court, GG Technologies alleged that Apple’s NameDrop infringes its Indian patent on technology that helps phones exchange contact details with nearby devices without requiring manual pairing. The manufacturer introduced StayTouch in 2019, the same year it first sought patent protection for the technology in the U.S. It filed its Indian patent application in 2021 and received the patent in July 2024.

    According to recent reports, apple introduced NameDrop as part of iOS 17 in June 2023. The feature debuted on iPhones later that year, with support for compatible Apple Watches arriving in October through watchOS 10.1.

    “We are seeking an injunction to restrict the usage of the NameDrop feature which is native to iOS,” GG Technologies told TechCrunch. GG Technologies urged the court in its filing to restrict Apple from selling or importing iPhones and Apple Watches preloaded with NameDrop in India. The case has yet to be listed for a hearing.

    It has been revealed that in the U.S., the International Trade Commission opened an investigation into Apple’s alleged patent infringement in August, following a complaint from GG Technologies. The startup is seeking an order that could block imports of infringing Apple devices into the country, along with restrictions on their sale.

    Founded in 2018 by Gaurav Goel, a graduate of the Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Delhi and a former Goldman Sachs investment banker, GG Technologies developed StayTouch as an alternative to exchanging business cards. The app is available on iOS and Android.

    Apple did not respond to a request for comment.

    Sources indicate that india has become increasingly crucial to Apple, both as a fast-growing consumer market and a major manufacturing hub outside China. The Cupertino manufacturer has expanded its retail presence in the South Asian nation, where iPhones still account for less than 10% of smartphone shipments, giving considerable room for growth.

    • CNN first reported the letter’s existence.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The representative in the US House expected to chair the House Intelligence Committee in January, Jim Himes (D-Conn.), has threatened to withhold support for funding government-owned systems from SpaceX amid the ongoing inquiry into the use of Starshield in Ukraine.

    In a recent development, “SpaceX’s potentially unilateral modification of a U.S. Government contract, combined with its lack of responsiveness to congressional oversight, calls into question every contract the U.S. Government has with SpaceX,” Himes wrote in a letter to SpaceX founder Elon Musk on Friday.

    CNN first reported the letter’s existence. The network also reported that Himes sent a classified communication to Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton with a similar message that it would be difficult for Congress to authorize funding for systems with SpaceX as the primary vendor.

    Industry observers note that spaceX has developed the consumer Starlink service over the last decade, which provides high-speed Internet from low-Earth orbit to user terminals on Earth. For government customers, SpaceX has also developed Starshield, a suite of satellite services that includes a militarized version of Starlink communications. The US government has purchased Starshield services and extended access to Ukraine, although the terms governing that access are largely classified.

    During the last several weeks, a controversy has erupted over interruptions to Starshield service in parts of Ukraine, cutting off connectivity to drones used to defend against Russian attacks.

    On October 19, for example, Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy stated of Starshield on social media, “Unfortunately, we have established that the equipment stops functioning at speeds of 130–161 kilometers per hour in various sectors of the front. This is slowing down our frontline logistics and limiting the use of various types of drones, particularly mid-strike drones and interceptors of jet-powered ‘shaheds.’” Additional disruptions were reported a week ago.

    Industry observers note that the central question is who decided to curtail the performance of Starshield assets in Ukraine. Accounts have variously implicated Musk, SpaceX, the Pentagon, and the White House. Musk has remarked that US officials control Starshield access, while defending SpaceX’s right to restrict the use of commercial Starlink service in war.

    “My ask to you is straightforward,” Himes wrote to Musk. “Explain the changes that were made to the Starshield service in October 2026, why those changes were made, and whether those changes were made unilaterally by SpaceX or were directed by a U.S. Government official.”.

    The communications from Himes suggest that Congressional Democrats, who will control the House and Senate in January following decisive victories in the Midterm elections, are prepared to not just investigate the disruption of these SpaceX services in Ukraine, but to take action that could threaten SpaceX’s broader national security business.

    “It is difficult for me to continue supporting the authorization of funding for these SpaceX-developed, government-owned systems, until I receive satisfactory answers to my questions about the Starshield service in Ukraine,” Himes wrote in his letter to Musk.

    According to recent reports, various options are open to Congressional Democrats, as well as some Republicans who have raised similar concerns, including demanding classified briefings and documents and restricting funding through appropriations to the US Department of Defense and other federal departments. Notably, the US Space Force awarded SpaceX a $2.29 billion contract earlier this year to develop the Space Data Network Backbone intended to support the Golden Dome missile defense initiative. That program, along with SpaceX’s work building intelligence satellites for the National Reconnaissance Office, could become a focus of congressional scrutiny.

    Sources indicate that it seems unlikely that the US government would sever ties with SpaceX for space-based data services or introduces, as the manufacturer is right now providing capabilities that no other US company can match. But Democrats are clearly serious about putting restrictions on Musk’s ability to influence geopolitical conflicts that have traditionally been the purview of governments rather than corporations.

    #70168. Tech Report: ‘Weak and dizzy’: the secretive ICE force-feeding tactics that ended a Cuban father’s hunger strike

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2568 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Theguardian ↗ Open Full Page

    Tech Report: ‘Weak and dizzy’: the secretive ICE force-feeding tactics that ended a Cuban father’s hunger strike

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2568 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theguardian

    ⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Exclusive: Luis Alejandro Cora Pérez says in messages to Guardian from inside Texas facility pain of force-feeding caused him to break strike.
    • It has been revealed that the text message that came from inside the Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention center was stark: “I have spent five days eating regular food.
    • A Cuban asylum seeker, Luis Alejandro Cora Pérez, 32, noted in messages to the Guardian this month that he was still weak and dizzy after three months without eating, but that he had broken his hunger strike because being force-fed was just too painful.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Exclusive: Luis Alejandro Cora Pérez says in messages to Guardian from inside Texas facility pain of force-feeding caused him to break strike.

    It has been revealed that the text message that came from inside the Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention center was stark: “I have spent five days eating regular food. If I don’t eat it, they put the tube in me to feed me.”.

    A Cuban asylum seeker, Luis Alejandro Cora Pérez, 32, noted in messages to the Guardian this month that he was still weak and dizzy after three months without eating, but that he had broken his hunger strike because being force-fed was just too painful.

    Sources indicate that the Trump administration responded to requests for comment by denying it had force-fed Cora Pérez. But the detainee sent more details – and his is far from an isolated case.

    Cora Pérez was one of two men on hunger striker at a Texas facility for whom ICE sought and received a federal judge’s permission to force-feed in recent weeks, a Guardian investigation found.

    Cora Pérez and the other man were locked up inside the Port Isabel service processing center, an ICE detention facility in south Texas, just a few miles from the US-Mexico border, on the coast near where Elon Musk’s SpaceX rolls out rockets. Cora Pérez began a hunger strike in August to protest against his prolonged detention by federal immigration officials while his case plays out. At first he only drank water, then after three weeks, he says he began to drink one Ensure nutritional shake per day.

    On 30 October, court records show ICE received permission to forcibly feed and hydrate him, and to restrain him while doing so.

    The next day he claims six guards at the center held him down, while medical staffers inserted a feeding tube through his nose and down his throat, and pumped nutritional liquid into his stomach – a process he called “traumatizing, both physically and psychologically”.

    Recent findings suggest that on 3 November, ICE then received permission from a federal judge to force-feed another hunger striker at Port Isabel, from Uzbekistan, federal court records show. The DHS notes the Uzbek man has not been subjected to the practice, however.

    According to recent reports, on Wednesday night, after weeks of communications, Cora Pérez was suddenly transferred to another detention center in Texas. His relative says neither of them were alerted to any aims to transfer him, or a reason for it.

    The DHS did not specify why Cora Pérez was transferred, adding that ICE makes custody determinations on a “case-by-case” basis based on “various factors”.

    The revelations come as ICE’s detention practices continue to come under fire amid allegations of mistreatment, and as an increasing number of sporadic hunger strikes have been breaking out in ICE facilities across the country.

    Sources indicate that the two men’s cases in Texas, revealed here for the first time, are some of the most recent instances of government lawyers seeking a federal judge’s permission, as required by ICE policy, and receiving the go-ahead to force-feed detained hunger strikers. The Guardian’s reporting is based on court records, interviews, dozens of messages exchanged and an interview conducted with Cora Pérez via a facility phone. It further reveals how the Trump administration is increasingly obtaining such court orders to force-feed detained immigrants, a secretive practice widely condemned as torture by human rights organizations and medical ethics groups.

    Detainees driven to hunger strike are typically using it as a last resort to protest against poor conditions and the Trump administration’s preference for arrest and prolonged detention while their civil immigration cases proceed through the system.

    Cora Pérez stated detention center staff inserted the feeding tube and left it in his body, a not uncommon practice, according to experts, and introduced nutrition – first a “clear liquid”, followed by a “milky liquid”, he recalled – through the tube twice more that day, before he cracked and said he broke his hunger strike, citing what he called “horrific torture”. He began voluntarily drinking nutritional shakes the following day, he said.

    “ICE does not hold back on anything, and they do anything they want, like we have seen, even killing their own US citizens,” he wrote to the Guardian, referring to the fatal shootings of Renee Good by an ICE officer and Alex Pretti by a border patrol officer in January of this year during Trump’s pivotal immigration crackdown on Minneapolis.

    In a recent development, detained hunger strikers subjected to involuntary medical procedures, including force-feeding, have rarely spoken out about their cases or revealed their identities, much less while still detained. Cora Pérez’s messages offer a rare glimpse at conditions inside a detention center’s restricted medical unit where hunger strikers and suicidal detainees are held.

    “They just took [the Uzbek man] in an ambulance after [him] fainting in front of the medical lobby where they take our vitals, our weight and our temperature,” Cora Pérez mentioned in an alarmed message last Monday morning.

    The Uzbek man was returned the following day to the facility, Cora Pérez said.

    “I see him every day because I see him in the room in front of me, but they don’t let us talk to each other,” he added.

    Recent findings suggest that the Guardian independently confirmed the Uzbek’s man identity but is not publicly naming him, because efforts to contact him have been unsuccessful. The man arrived at the Mexico-US border in April 2022 and was released into the country while navigating his immigration case. He was arrested by border patrol officials in April of this year and placed in detention. The man does not appear to have any criminal record and the DHS did not point to any criminal history.

    In a statement, DHS remarked that after they received the court’s permission to force-feed the Uzbek man, he “has voluntarily taken in fluids and there has been NO force-feeding or forced hydration”.

    Security operations at the sprawling Port Isabel facility in Los Fresnos, Texas, are run by a private prison manufacturer, Akima Global Services, while healthcare is primarily handled by government workers.

    Industry observers note that “ICE respects detainees’ rights to exercise self-expression and medical autonomy by refusing nourishment and medical care,” the DHS mentioned in a statement. “ICE Health Services Corps may provide involuntary medical treatment only to prevent imminent life-threatening harm or death. Medical staff may provide treatment only to medically stabilize the patient, bringing the detainee outside the imminent harm, incapacitation, or death.”.

    It has been revealed that the US attorney’s office in the southern district of Texas, which represented ICE in its force-feeding request, did not respond to multiple requests for comment. Virginia-headquartered Akima Global Services, and its parent tech giant Nana Regional Corporation, based in Alaska, did not respond to a request for comment.

    According to recent reports, force-feeding cases are shrouded in secrecy. After a detainee debuts a hunger strike, ICE often sequesters them in medical isolation cells for monitoring, according to ICE’s detention standards. The DHS noted that ICE continues to offer hunger strikers three meals per day.

    According to recent reports, after a certain period of not eating, which varies per case, ICE will request a federal judge’s permission to force-feed the hunger striker. Many court records, and sometimes entire court dockets, are sealed and hidden from public view. In Cora Pérez and the Uzbek man’s cases, like in others, they did not have any legal representation to challenge the force-feeding requests.

    The Guardian found at least five instances in which ICE requested permission to force-feed hunger strikers in Port Isabel since January 2025. The federal judge who ruled on Cora Perez and the Uzbek man, Rolando Olvera, has similarly ordered in at least three other cases, records show. Olvera’s judicial assistant mentioned the court had no comment for this article.

    Sources indicate that ICE is known to have requested permission to force-feed at least 21 detainees across the US since January 2025, the Guardian found, but the number is probably higher since an unknown number of records and dockets remain sealed, unsearchable and not feasible to locate. Most of the cases coinciding with the second Trump administration and tracked by the Guardian are in Texas and Florida, with others in Georgia, Arizona and Washington state. Under the Biden administration, ICE force-feeding requests were also made in Louisiana and California.

    Amy Zeidan, an emergency medicine physician based in Atlanta and an expert on healthcare in immigration detention, stated force-feeding hunger strikers can amount to “torture”, and lead to significant psychological distress. She also said it was a violation of medical ethics.

    It has been revealed that “Essentially it’s like inserting a straw into your nose,” Zeidan noted. “You have a gag reflex, so most times people will gag, and that’s really uncomfortable. And people will even vomit repeatedly if it continues to irritate their gag reflex.”.

    Zeidan added that the forceful insertion of a feeding tube can lead to the swelling of the nostrils and the throat, and even tear them, leading to bleeding.

    Sources indicate that “It is like torture – somebody is doing a painful procedure to you that you don’t consent to,” Zeidan added. “Autonomy is a fundamental principle of medical ethics. We can’t do something to patients if they don’t want to, even if we think it’s good for them.”.

    There are numerous cells and rooms inside the Port Isabel medical unit, including isolation cells and shared rooms for ill detainees, according to Cora Pérez. In recent weeks, there were five people in the Port Isabel medical isolation cells used for hunger striking or suicidal detainees, he added. He described the cells as “practically freezing”, constantly surveilled with a security camera, and with just a bed, toilet and sink. As well as himself, he says he observed the Uzbek man, a Middle Eastern man, a “tall” eastern European man and a Black man of unknown nationality in the isolation cells. Unit detainees are escorted by facility staff to showers and sometimes receive yard and television access, he remarked.

    According to recent reports, cora Pérez worries for the other detainees. The Black man, whose identity or nationality he does not know, seems to have “serious mental health problems”, Cora Pérez observed.

    “He harms himself and spends the night yelling and hitting the door, and does not let anyone sleep,” he said.

    Sources indicate that the Guardian has independently confirmed the eastern European and Middle Eastern men’s identities, but is not publicly naming them because efforts to contact them have been unsuccessful. The DHS did not comment on the other men inside the medical isolation unit, saying they could not comment without the Guardian providing their identities.

    Recent findings suggest that cora Pérez had left his son and parents in Cuba and requested asylum at the Mexico-US border in 2023, according to a relative who spoke to the Guardian on condition of anonymity due to fear of retaliation by immigration authorities. Cora Pérez went to live with the relative in Florida, where he worked in maintenance at a hotel and as a food delivery worker, he remarked.

    Industry observers note that in March 2025, Cora Pérez was arrested by local police and later convicted of two misdemeanors, including “breach of peace” and “obstructing an officer without violence”, according to local records. He was sentenced to two months in jail, his relative remarked. But ICE placed a hold on him and as he was being released in June 2025, immigration officials took him into custody – a common system – and soon transferred him to the Adelanto detention center, a privately-run facility in California.

    Days in Adelanto turned to weeks, then months, then over a year, according to a federal court order denying one of his petitions requesting his release. His multiple requests to immigration and ordinary federal courts for release from detention, while he fights his asylum case, have been unsuccessful.

    Sources indicate that “All his claims will be heard by an immigration judge, and he will receive due process. This administration will not ignore the rule of law,” DHS stated. “Criminal illegal aliens are not welcome in the US.”.

    In August, he stopped eating to protest against his protracted detention.

    Industry observers note that “I have spent two birthdays behind ICE’s bars,” he wrote. “The reasons I did the hunger strike in Adelanto are for my political asylum, for the time I have spent detained, [and] because I have a 14-year-old son who is starving to death in Cuba because he does not have my help.

    “Also due to the mistreatment by the officials,” he added.

    Cora Pérez did not tell his family about the hunger strike, so as not to further worry them. It was not until he was transferred to Port Isabel in late September that he confessed to his relative he had been on a prolonged hunger strike.

    “He doesn’t share details so that I won’t get upset or worry,” the relative said in a phone interview.

    In a recent development, cora Pérez’s mother, who is in Cuba, “does not know anything, because she is sick, and with his detention she has gotten worse”, the relative added, between tears. “I don’t want her nor his grandmother to know anything about it,” the relative added.

    On 30 October, the federal prosecutors requested permission for ICE to forcibly feed and hydrate Cora Pérez. Hours later, a federal judge approved the procedures without hearing from Cora Pérez. Cora Pérez told the Guardian in various instances he felt it was unfair he was not given the opportunity to present his case to the judge before the judge approved his force-feeding.

    Sources indicate that “It’s very disturbing because the judge is basically making a decision on information that is only provided by one side,” remarked Linus Chan, a professor of clinical law and the director of the detainee rights clinic at the University of Minnesota law school. “That just seems ridiculous.”.

    Cora Pérez was force-fed the following day, he mentioned in his messages and in a phone call, adding that he did not physically resist because he “had seen a lot of mistreatment of others detained”.

    Industry observers note that “[ICE does] what they want with us, whatever they want, because a federal judge gave them permission,” he added. “I have suffered on the island [of Cuba] and now at the hands of ICE.”.

    After asking Cora Pérez about the DHS’s denials that he was force-fed, he repeated that he was. “Brother, ICE states and does whatever they want. They deny, punish, retaliate and do everything at their own will. They have even sent Cubans to Africa,” he noted.

    It has been revealed that the number of people detained by ICE has soared under the Trump administration. And due to policy and legal changes, tens of thousands of people are forced to stay in detention for long periods while they fight their immigration cases.

    Recent findings suggest that chan, from the University of Minnesota, states prolonged detention and delays in their cases lead to logical conclusion. “That’s exactly when people protest,” he noted.

    “And the only form of protest, for many of these people, is a hunger strike,” he stated.

    As Trump’s hardline immigration crackdown continues and people are detained as a first resort while their cases play out, Chan said: “Hunger strikes will become more common.”.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • A Russian helicopter is suspected of violating Finnish airspace, the Nordic country's Ministry of Defense said Saturday.
    • The incident happened a few hours after a drone attack left a Russian cargo ship ablaze in the Gulf of Finland, the easternmost part of the Baltic Sea.
    • According to Finland's Defense Ministry, the incursion happened at 12:34 p.m.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A Russian helicopter is suspected of violating Finnish airspace, the Nordic country's Ministry of Defense said Saturday.

    The incident happened a few hours after a drone attack left a Russian cargo ship ablaze in the Gulf of Finland, the easternmost part of the Baltic Sea.

    According to Finland's Defense Ministry, the incursion happened at 12:34 p.m. local time (10:34 UTC/GMT) off the town of Loviisa, on the southern coast.

    "This alleged airspace violation may be linked to rescue or surveillance operations carried out by Finland following damage sustained by a cargo ship in the Gulf of Finland," public broadcaster YLE cited Defense Minister Antti Hakkanen as saying.

    The ministry added the helicopter could have penetrated up to 4.1 kilometers (2.5 miles) into Finnish territory.

    Earlier Saturday, Finland — one of NATO's newest members — said a Russian cargo ship heading for Russia's Baltic exclave of Kaliningrad caught fire after being struck by drones in the Gulf of Finland.

    The Finnish military stated the Sparta II was damaged ⁠west ⁠of Russia's Gogland island, about 40 kilometers (25 miles) from Finland's coast, and later drifted into Finnish territorial waters.

    Finnish ‌Border ​Guard Commander Ilja Iljin later told YLE that the vessel, which is known to have links to the Russian military, was struck by Ukrainian  drones while in Russian waters.

    "At the moment, ​there is no confirmed information ⁠about ​what cargo ​is on board, ​but it ‌cannot be ruled out ​that ⁠there is military materiel on ⁠board," ​Iljin mentioned.

    The ship is on a US sanctions list, according to a search of the Open Sanctions website.

    The Border Guard later stated the crew of the Sparta II was evacuating into a life raft and rescue boat.

    "The [Ukraine] war is spilling over into our neighbouring areas," wrote Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo on X.

    Ukraine has the right to fight against the aggressor," he added.

    The Finnish government has put temporary curbs on aviation and maritime traffic in the eastern Gulf of Finland.

    The Defense Ministry noted Finland had informed its allies about the incident.
